What the fight over Peru pension laws is about

Under President Keiko Fujimori’s new government, Finance Minister Elmer Cuba is preparing formal constitutional challenges — demandas de inconstitucionalidad — at Peru’s Constitutional Court. The targets are four spending laws approved by the previous Congress. These are not technical tweaks; they are major, recurring commitments the new economic team says were enacted without funding.

The four laws are Ley 32581 (teacher pensions), Ley 32561 (military and police pensions), Ley 32563 (bonus and CTS payments for CAS contract workers), and Ley 32424 (a CAFAE incentive for DL 276 regime workers). The two pension laws carry the biggest price tags. The MEF puts the teacher-pension law at roughly S/8 billion a year — about US$2.4 billion — for more than 160,000 retired and former teachers. The military and police pension law is far larger over time: the Fiscal Council and the MEF estimate its cost at around S/46 billion in present value, or about US$13.6 billion — the full future liability, not a single year’s bill.

The government’s argument

Minister Cuba has been blunt. In his own words: “El Congreso no tiene en ninguna parte del mundo desarrollado la iniciativa de gasto. El gasto lo maneja el Ejecutivo.” That translates as: Congress has no spending initiative anywhere in the developed world; the Executive manages spending. It is a direct challenge to the legislature’s role in setting fiscal policy. Cuba has said the government picked the four laws that “pueden mover la aguja” — that can move the needle — on the public accounts.

The MEF’s position is that these laws undermine the fiscal rule Peru has used for years to keep its finances credible. The new Fujimori government leans toward fiscal discipline and has staffed the economic team with pro-market figures. It views the laws as unfunded mandates that would eventually force tax hikes, more debt, or cuts elsewhere.

Why this matters for investors and the region

Peru has long been a poster child for fiscal discipline in Latin America — low debt, a strong central bank, and steady investment. That reputation is now being tested, and the test is structural: who really decides how public money is spent, the Executive or Congress? If the government’s challenges succeed, it reinforces the idea that Peru’s fiscal anchors hold. If they fail, it sets a precedent where the legislature can pass expensive laws without the government’s sign-off — the kind of thing that pressures a country’s credit rating.

Peru still runs one of the lowest public-debt ratios in Latin America — a big reason it holds an investment-grade credit rating that keeps its borrowing costs down. That standing is the asset the MEF says it is defending. A steady run of costly, unfunded laws is exactly the kind of drift that erodes it over time, and rating agencies watch these fights closely.

If you hold Peruvian assets, or regional funds that include them, that is the signal to watch. It also shows how the Fujimori government will handle an opposition-leaning Congress that still holds real institutional power — and whether Lima’s reputation for keeping spending in check survives its first real test of the new term.

What happens next

The Constitutional Court will first decide whether to admit the challenges, then rule on the merits — a process that can take months. No case number or filing date has been reported yet. In the meantime, the politics are heating up: teachers’ unions are already defending Ley 32581 as the correction of a historical injustice and a path to dignified pensions after decades of service. That is a powerful counter-narrative, and it will not be easy for the government to face down.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which four laws is Peru’s MEF challenging? The four laws are Ley 32581 on teacher pensions, Ley 32561 on military and police pensions, Ley 32563 on bonuses and CTS for CAS contract workers, and Ley 32424 on a CAFAE incentive homologation. All were passed by the previous Congress and now face constitutional challenges. How much do the pension laws cost? The MEF puts the teacher-pension law at about S/8 billion a year, roughly US$2.4 billion, for more than 160,000 retired teachers. The military and police pension law is estimated at around S/46 billion in present value, about US$13.6 billion, by the Fiscal Council and the MEF. These figures come from the government and its fiscal watchdog. What does the government want the court to do? The government wants the Constitutional Court to declare the laws unconstitutional, arguing that Congress cannot create spending obligations on its own. The MEF says the laws threaten the fiscal rule and could strain public accounts.

Sources: El Popular; Gestión; La República; Infobae Perú; Peru’s Consejo Fiscal and Ministry of Economy and Finance (MEF).

World.title: El Niño Turns Central America’s Dry Corridor Into a Hunger Zone
World.content:
Central America · Climate

Key Facts Guatemala hunger 3.2 million people — about 17% — face acute food insecurity in July–September 2026, per SESAN.

3.2 million people — about 17% — face acute food insecurity in July–September 2026, per SESAN. Honduras crisis 1.8 million already affected, and up to 2.2 million possible by year-end, per UNAH.

1.8 million already affected, and up to 2.2 million possible by year-end, per UNAH. Global warning A stronger El Niño could add 49 million people to acute hunger worldwide, per the WFP.

A stronger El Niño could add 49 million people to acute hunger worldwide, per the WFP. Regional reach More than 16 million people affected in Latin America and the Caribbean, with Central America the sharpest riser, per the WFP.

More than 16 million people affected in Latin America and the Caribbean, with Central America the sharpest riser, per the WFP. Emergency declared Marcovia, in southern Honduras, cited 15,000 families hit by drought and crop loss.

Marcovia, in southern Honduras, cited 15,000 families hit by drought and crop loss. Livestock losses More than 400 cattle have died in southern Honduras, reports La Prensa.

Drought is tightening across Central America’s Dry Corridor, and failed harvests are turning hunger into an everyday reality.

If you follow Latin American markets or live in the region, the El Niño food crisis deserves your attention now. The parched fields of Honduras and Guatemala are already feeding through to grocery bills, migration pressure and regional stability — and the worst of the lean season is still ahead.

Illustrative: drought-cracked farmland, the daily reality across the Dry Corridor. (Photo: Friedrich Haag, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What is happening in the Dry Corridor

The Dry Corridor runs through Guatemala, Honduras, El Salvador and Nicaragua — a strip of land that has always known tough farming. But this El Niño is landing at the worst possible moment, bringing drought, erratic rains and extreme heat just as farmers should be planting maize and beans.

In Guatemala, the food-security secretariat SESAN, using the IPC/CIF phase scale, projects 3.2 million people — about 17% of the population — in acute food insecurity between July and September 2026. In practice that means skipping meals, selling off animals or tools, and eating less to get by.

In Honduras, the crisis is already here. The food-security observatory at UNAH, the national university, estimated on August 6, 2026 that 1.8 million people face a food crisis today, a figure that could climb to 2.2 million by year-end if the rains stay away. These are families farming small hillside plots, dependent on a single harvest to eat for the year.

What the El Niño food crisis looks like on the ground

Talk to farmers in southern Honduras and you hear the same thing. The corn is stunted, the bean plants are withered, the wells are drying up. On August 5, 2026, the municipality of Marcovia in Choluteca declared a state of emergency for more than 15,000 families hit by water shortages and crop losses.

Honduras’s emergency agency COPECO has put 75 municipalities on yellow alert and 49 on green alert — a sign the strain is spreading well beyond one district. La Prensa reported on August 5, 2026 that the drought has already killed more than 400 head of cattle, and warned of higher prices for grains, milk and meat in the months ahead if the rains do not return.

This is not just a bad season. FEWS NET’s El Niño 2026–2027 outlook flags the Dry Corridor as a zone of concern. The region is still recovering from earlier climate shocks, and high fuel and fertilizer prices make it far harder for small farmers to bounce back. They are caught in a trap: no rain to grow food, and no money to buy it.

Why this matters for Latin America and investors

A drought in rural Honduras is not a local footnote. The Dry Corridor is a major source of staple food for the region, so when maize and bean harvests fail, prices climb in markets from Guatemala City to San Pedro Sula. That hits urban families too, and feeds inflation in economies that are already stretched.

There is also a slower consequence: migration. Drought, crop loss, poverty and hunger are well-documented drivers of migration pressure from the region — when people cannot feed their children, they move. That means more strain on borders and more political noise across the hemisphere. For investors, the takeaway is plain: Central American food supply chains are exposed to climate shocks, and prices can spike fast. The WFP warned around August 5–6, 2026 that a strengthening El Niño could push an extra 49 million people worldwide into acute food insecurity, lifting the global total to about 274 million by the end of 2027. For Latin America and the Caribbean, it put the figure at more than 16 million people affected, with Central America projected to see the largest proportional increase. That is not a distant scenario — it is happening now.

Aid agencies are already repositioning. The WFP says it is scaling up preparedness across the region, and Honduras has begun channelling emergency support to the hardest-hit municipalities. But funding for these responses is chronically tight, and the lean season — when last year’s stocks run out before the new harvest — is only beginning. The next rains, or their absence, will decide how deep this crisis runs.

Frequently Asked Questions

Which countries are most affected by the El Niño food crisis? Guatemala and Honduras are the hardest hit this cycle, across the Dry Corridor. Guatemala’s SESAN projects 3.2 million people in acute food insecurity between July and September 2026, and UNAH estimates 1.8 million in Honduras, potentially rising to 2.2 million by year-end. How does El Niño cause food shortages? El Niño shifts weather patterns, bringing drought to some areas and heavy rain to others. In the Dry Corridor it means below-average rainfall and higher temperatures, which damage maize and bean harvests. FEWS NET adds that weak recovery from earlier shocks and high fuel and fertilizer prices make the impact worse. What is the global scale of this El Niño event? The WFP estimates that a strengthening El Niño could push an additional 49 million people worldwide into acute food insecurity, bringing the global total to about 274 million by the end of 2027. In Latin America and the Caribbean, it expects more than 16 million people affected, with Central America seeing the largest proportional rise.

Sources: Guatemala’s SESAN (IPC/CIF); OBSAN-UNAH (Honduras); UN World Food Programme; FEWS NET; COPECO; La Prensa (Honduras).

World.title: Why Banxico’s New Bond Tool Is Testing Its Autonomy
World.content:
Mexico · Economy

Key Facts Rate held Banxico kept its benchmark at 6.50% on Aug 6, 2026, in a unanimous vote.

Banxico kept its benchmark at 6.50% on Aug 6, 2026, in a unanimous vote. Inflation low July 2026 inflation fell to a six-year low, though the bank sees the next declines coming more slowly.

July 2026 inflation fell to a six-year low, though the bank sees the next declines coming more slowly. New power From Aug 17, Banxico can buy up to 100 billion pesos (about US$5.8 billion) of Cetes and Bondes F per quarter.

From Aug 17, Banxico can buy up to 100 billion pesos (about US$5.8 billion) of Cetes and Bondes F per quarter. Secondary only The purchases happen in the secondary market to ease temporary liquidity shortages — not to finance the government.

The purchases happen in the secondary market to ease temporary liquidity shortages — not to finance the government. Legal firewall Article 28 of the Constitution and Articles 11 and 12 of the Banxico Law still bar direct government financing.

Article 28 of the Constitution and Articles 11 and 12 of the Banxico Law still bar direct government financing. Board intact Governor Victoria Rodríguez Ceja led the five-member board, with no dissent and no political pressure.

A new emergency tool tests how the market reads Mexico’s central bank independence — but the legal guardrails, specialists say, are still firmly in place.

You may have seen headlines suggesting Mexico’s central bank just cracked open the door to government meddling. That is not what happened. This is a new liquidity tool, and it helps to understand why it does not erode Banxico autonomy. Since 1994, the bank has run independently, and a constitutional ban on directly financing the government still holds. The new power, effective Aug 17, 2026, lets the bank buy up to 100 billion pesos (about US$5.8 billion) of Cetes and Bondes F each quarter — but only on the secondary market, and only to relieve temporary cash shortages. That is a long way from printing money to cover the budget.

The Banco de México headquarters in Mexico City. (Photo: ProtoplasmaKid, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

What the new tool means for Banxico autonomy

Here is the short version: Banxico autonomy is not being eroded, according to most specialists who have read the measure. The tool works like the exchange commission’s dollar auctions — used only in specific, stressed moments, not as a daily habit. Luis Gonzalí drew that comparison, noting that months can pass between uses. Barclays analysts stress the bank “cannot flood the system with liquidity,” because the constitutional limits still bind. The market’s nervous reaction, economist Gabriela Siller notes, simply shows that investors pay close attention to what the central bank does — which is healthy, not alarming.

Skeptics exist. Guillermo Barba has argued that once a central bank grants itself a power this large, the real question is no longer whether it will use it, but when. It is a fair point about precedent. But note the context: there is no statement from President Claudia Sheinbaum or the Finance Ministry attacking the bank’s independence — no political pressure, no attempted takeover. The worry is about perception, in a market already watchful after Mexico’s judicial reform. For now, there is no concrete spillover into Banxico’s governance.

Timing is part of why this gets read so closely. Mexico’s overhaul of its courts — including electing judges by popular vote — has left some investors uneasy about the strength of the country’s institutions. In that climate, anything that could blur the line between the central bank and the government draws sharper scrutiny than it would in calmer times. That is exactly why Banxico went out of its way to spell out the limits.

How the intervention actually works

Picture a bank that holds government bonds and suddenly needs cash. Normally it sells them. But in a panic, buyers vanish. Banxico can step in, buy the securities, hand over temporary cash, and sell them back later. That is a classic liquidity operation — not financing, because the government gets no new money. The trade sits between the central bank and market players such as banks, brokerages and pension funds, never with the Treasury. The 100 billion peso (about US$5.8 billion) quarterly cap — up to roughly 400 billion pesos (about US$23 billion) a year — is generous but bounded, and the prohibitions in Article 28 and Articles 11 and 12 stay untouched.

The timing helps explain the caution. July inflation hit a six-year low, yet Banxico expects the decline to slow, which is why it held rates at 6.50%. The new tool simply gives the bank another way to handle short-term market stress without touching rates — a technical upgrade, not a political one.

Why Latin American readers and investors should care

This is bigger than Mexico. Across the region, central banks live or die by credibility. If markets ever decided Banxico had been captured, the peso would weaken, bond yields would jump, and money would leave — and not only from Mexico, as investors re-rate the whole region. So this is a test of whether an independent bank can adopt a new tool without denting its mandate. Peers in Brazil, Colombia and Chile will be watching. If you hold pesos, reais or Chilean pesos, your returns rest on trust in these institutions.

The reassuring part: the safeguards are strong, and the people who follow this daily say autonomy holds. The signal to watch is simple — how often the tool is actually used. Rare, emergency-only use supports independence; frequent use would be the red flag.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does this let the government borrow money from Banxico? No. The law bars direct financing of the government. Purchases happen only in the secondary market, so Banxico buys securities from banks and funds, not from the Treasury, and the government receives no new money. Why is the market concerned if the rules are clear? Investors focus on perception and precedent. They worry that a large new power, even a well-guarded one, could be widened later. Analysts counter that the secondary-market-only scope and the constitutional limits keep that risk small. What should an investor watch to judge Banxico independence? Watch how often and how heavily the tool is used, and whether anyone moves to change Article 28 or the Banxico Law. Occasional use in genuine liquidity emergencies supports autonomy. Sustained or growing use would raise real concerns.

Sources: El Universal; Banco de México; Reuters; Bloomberg; Barclays; INEGI.

World.title: Indonesia Pitches a Mercosur Trade Deal, With Brazil as the Broker
World.content:
Brazil · Trade

Key Facts First step Indonesia proposed a narrow preferential trade agreement (PTA) with Mercosur at the BRICS Trade Ministers’ Meeting in Jaipur, India, on Aug 7, 2026.

Indonesia proposed a narrow preferential trade agreement (PTA) with Mercosur at the BRICS Trade Ministers’ Meeting in Jaipur, India, on Aug 7, 2026. Stalled CEPA The broader Indonesia-Mercosur Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement is stuck over how wide and deep the deal should be.

The broader Indonesia-Mercosur Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement is stuck over how wide and deep the deal should be. Consensus ask Jakarta asked Brazil to bridge differences and build alignment among Mercosur members on the PTA.

Jakarta asked Brazil to bridge differences and build alignment among Mercosur members on the PTA. Open response Brazil’s development, industry, trade and services minister, Márcio Elias Rosa, said Brasília will study the proposal.

Brazil’s development, industry, trade and services minister, Márcio Elias Rosa, said Brasília will study the proposal. Trade heft Indonesia-Brazil trade was about US$7 billion in 2025 and US$3.53 billion in the first half of 2026.

Indonesia-Brazil trade was about US$7 billion in 2025 and US$3.53 billion in the first half of 2026. Asia pivot Mercosur is already advancing deals with the EU and Japan and eyeing one with China as it diversifies away from US trade friction.

Indonesia wants a faster, narrower trade pact with South America’s big bloc — and it is asking Brazil to make it happen.

If you have been watching Mercosur’s busy year, you know the bloc has become the emerging world’s most sought-after trade partner. Now add Indonesia. In early August, Jakarta’s trade minister floated an Indonesia-Mercosur trade deal in slimmed-down form — skip the full agreement for now and do a smaller, quicker one instead. Nothing is signed. But it tells you a lot about where global trade is heading, and where your next opportunity might sit.

What Indonesia is proposing

Indonesia’s trade minister, Budi Santoso, used the BRICS Trade Ministers’ Meeting in Jaipur, India, to suggest a fresh path. His pitch was a preferential trade agreement, or PTA — a focused deal that cuts tariffs on a selected list of goods. Think of it as trade’s express lane — faster and easier than a sprawling comprehensive pact.

Why the change of tack? The bigger Indonesia-Mercosur Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement, or CEPA, has stalled. The problem is not Jakarta’s appetite — it is friction inside Mercosur over how broad the deal should be. So Indonesia asked Brazil for help. “We hope Brazil can help build consensus among Mercosur members and advance negotiations for the Indonesia-Mercosur PTA,” Santoso said. Brazil’s development, industry, trade and services minister, Márcio Elias Rosa, replied that Brasília is open to more talks and will study the proposal. No timeline was set. This is a proposal, not a deal.

What the Indonesia-Mercosur trade deal would cover

Here is where it gets interesting for commodities. Indonesia is the world’s biggest palm oil producer. Brazil and Argentina are soy oil powers. Those two oils compete head-to-head in global food and biofuel markets, and a PTA would help decide which one gets the tariff edge in the other’s backyard. A deal would likely cover tariffs on goods ranging from vegetable and animal fats to vehicles, electrical machinery, rubber, mineral fuels, sugar, cotton, tobacco and metal ores.

Look at the current picture. In the first half of 2026, Indonesia-Brazil trade reached US$3.53 billion. Indonesia sold Brazil about US$1.17 billion of goods — palm oil, vehicles and rubber — while buying roughly US$2.36 billion of Brazilian farm residues, sugar, cotton and ores. That leaves Jakarta with a deficit of about US$1.19 billion. A PTA is, in part, Indonesia’s attempt to rebalance that ledger by getting more of its products onto Brazilian shelves.

There is a bigger strategic thread here too. Indonesia has spent recent years chasing new markets to cut its reliance on China and the West — from a fresh pact with the EU to joining BRICS. Latin America is one of the last large regions where it has little preferential access. A Mercosur deal, even a narrow one, would plant a flag and give its exporters a foothold before rivals lock in their own terms.

Why Latin American readers should care

This is not just a Jakarta-Brasília affair. It is a window into Mercosur’s strategic pivot. The bloc is already living with the EU-Mercosur agreement, which took provisional effect on May 1, 2026. It launched talks with Japan in June, is eyeing a deal with China, and now Indonesia — a BRICS member since January 2025, with more than 280 million people — wants a foothold. That is a lot of suitors at one dance.

For Brazilian and Argentine agribusiness, the prize is Asian market access at preferential rates. For Indonesian palm oil, South America is a growing market and a hedge. And with the United States raising tariffs on major partners, every new Mercosur deal trims the bloc’s reliance on any single buyer. If you invest or live in the region, watch the farm supply chain: if this advances, expect ripples in vegetable-oil pricing and machinery flows.

What happens next

Do not expect a quick signature. Brazil has to study the proposal, then take it to Argentina, Paraguay, Uruguay and Bolivia — a full Mercosur member since 2024. Each has its own farm lobbies and industrial priorities, which is exactly why the CEPA stalled. The PTA route lowers the bar to a smaller menu of goods. Get consensus, and Indonesia is through the door; miss it, and the bigger deal stays parked. Either way, Southeast Asia is signalling that it is serious about Latin America.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Indonesia-Mercosur trade deal signed? No. It is a proposal. Indonesia suggested a PTA at the BRICS meeting in August 2026 as a first step toward a broader agreement. Brazil said it will study the idea. No timeline was set, and formal negotiations have not started. What is the difference between a PTA and a CEPA? A PTA is a narrow agreement that cuts tariffs on specific, selected goods, so it is quicker to negotiate. A CEPA is comprehensive, covering goods, services, investment and trade rules, which makes it far more complex and slower to finalize. Why does Indonesia want a deal with Mercosur? Indonesia wants preferential access for its palm oil, vehicles, rubber and machinery, while narrowing its trade deficit with Brazil. It also wants a foothold in South America as Mercosur signs deals with the EU, Japan and others. For a country of more than 280 million people, early access matters.

01 The session in one read

Copper futures, via the CPER tracking fund, settled at US$40.18 on Monday, a 0.70% rise that animated the largest mining listings in the Americas. The movement was neither frantic nor speculative; it was a methodical climb built on solid, if unglamorous, industrial consumption.

The two giants of the Andean copper belt moved in lockstep. Southern Copper, deeply embedded in Peru’s southern mining corridor and Mexico’s Sonora state, advanced 0.53% to US$200.11. Freeport-McMoRan, whose Cerro Verde operation in Peru ranks among the world’s biggest concentrating sites, rose 1.28% to US$70.51.

Assessment — Demand persistence, not a spike HIGH The session lacked a single explosive catalyst, which is precisely why the gains matter. Prices advanced because everyday demand from manufacturers and infrastructure builders remains resilient, not because of a temporary supply scare. This persistent bid, anchored in electrification and Chinese factory activity, rewarded patient holders of miners like Freeport-McMoRan and Southern Copper. The variable to watch is any shift in China’s fiscal support for grid spending, as that flow of orders is the quiet engine beneath the copper market right now.

02 The board

The trio of copper proxies flashed uniformly green on Monday. The CPER fund, designed to mirror futures contracts rather than physical metal, printed US$40.18 at the settlement. The gain of 0.70% set the pace for mining equities, which typically amplify the commodity’s moves.

Southern Copper’s US$200.11 close was the more muted of the two, its 0.53% gain trailing Freeport-McMoRan’s 1.28% rise to US$70.51. Both stocks sit on vast proven and probable copper reserves across Chile and Peru, making their daily swings a reliable barometer of investor conviction in the industrial metal’s trajectory.

03 What moved it

The session’s primary driver was the enduring pull of Chinese demand. Order books for copper-intensive goods, from electric wiring to transformers, remained full as state-backed infrastructure programs kept consumption steady. This wasn’t a speculative frenzy triggered by a single policy announcement, but rather the hum of regular procurement.

Layered on top was the energy transition’s insatiable appetite for copper. Wind turbines, solar farms, and a growing fleet of electric vehicles require multiples more of the metal than their fossil-fuel equivalents. Monday’s incremental price rise captured that slow-building structural deficit, which continues to absorb supply even when other commodities face headwinds.

04 The Latin American read

For Chile and Peru, Monday’s equity board translated a quiet day in the pits into measurable national wealth. Chile, the world’s top copper producer, sees its fiscal resources tied directly to the metal’s fortunes, and a rising CPER and Southern Copper share price feeds directly into the outlook for Santiago’s spending plans.

Peru, the number-three supplier globally, felt the session through Southern Copper and Freeport-McMoRan’s extensive local operations. The 0.53% gain in Southern Copper, a company with immense reserves in Peru’s Arequipa and Moquegua regions, lifted the entire mining-weighted Lima exchange in after-market sentiment, reinforcing the country’s deep economic link to the red metal.

05 The names to watch

Southern Copper, now trading at US$200.11 after a 0.53% daily climb, remains the purest large-cap play on Andean copper. Its low-cost production profile across Peru and Mexico makes its share price acutely responsive to even modest futures advances.

Freeport-McMoRan, at US$70.51, adds a global dimension with large-scale leaching and milling operations in South America and North America. Its 1.28% gain reflects not just copper’s direction but also confidence in stable operational permits and disciplined capital spending across its Cerro Verde and Grasberg interests.

06 The outlook

Copper’s ability to rise without a crisis catalyst signals a market that is structurally tight. With Chinese grid investment pressuring daily supply and no major mine ramp-up imminent in Chile or Peru, the path of least resistance for CPER and its associated miners appears gently upward, barring a sudden macroeconomic shock.

07 What to watch

Chinese grid-ordering data: Any uptick or downtick in China’s State Grid procurement will move copper directly, as it remains the single largest institutional buyer of refined copper wire and cable.

Any uptick or downtick in China’s State Grid procurement will move copper directly, as it remains the single largest institutional buyer of refined copper wire and cable. Peruvian community negotiations: Southern Copper’s projects in Arequipa and Moquegua frequently face community dialogue; a disruption would tighten the supply picture and could send Freeport-McMoRan’s shares higher on scarcity.

Southern Copper’s projects in Arequipa and Moquegua frequently face community dialogue; a disruption would tighten the supply picture and could send Freeport-McMoRan’s shares higher on scarcity. Energy transition bill of materials: Quarterly updates from wind, solar and EV manufacturers on copper content per unit will signal whether structural demand is still accelerating or plateauing.

Quarterly updates from wind, solar and EV manufacturers on copper content per unit will signal whether structural demand is still accelerating or plateauing. Chilean constitutional mining debate: Any revival of royalty or nationalisation discussions in Santiago would immediately affect Southern Copper’s risk premium and alter the regional investment case for copper majors.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did copper rise on Monday?

The CPER fund gained 0.70% to US$40.18 because steady Chinese industrial buying and ongoing energy-transition orders kept demand firm, lifting futures and mining shares in tandem.

How did Southern Copper perform?

Southern Copper added 0.53% to US$200.11 on Monday, trailing Freeport-McMoRan among major copper miners for the session, driven by its deep exposure to Peruvian and Mexican production.

What is CPER?

CPER is an exchange-traded fund that tracks copper futures rather than the spot price of physical copper; its Monday settlement was US$40.18, reflecting a 0.70% daily increase in the futures market.

Are Chile and Peru still the top copper producers?

Yes, Chile is the world’s number-one copper producer and Peru ranks third, behind the Democratic Republic of the Congo; together they supply a large portion of the global concentrate, making Monday’s share moves in Southern Copper and Freeport-McMoRan particularly relevant for Latin American investors.

Today’s Focus The S&P/BMV IPC softened 0.75% to 66,439 points on Monday, failing to hold the 67,000 mark as a sell-off in retail and infrastructure stocks outpaced modest gains in telecoms. Walmex tumbled 2.9% and airport group GAP lost 3.2%, while the peso barely moved, nudging 0.04% weaker to 17.14 per dollar. Trading was defensive and thin. Investors avoided large bets with a critical US consumer-price reading due Wednesday, which will refine bets on Federal Reserve rate cuts. A gentle firming in the DXY index to 99.75 kept the peso pinned, though Banxico officials continued to warn that the inflation fight is not yet won. The standout domestic story was retail. Walmex slumped on light $14 million turnover, reversing a relief rally from last week, while Femsa’s trading units fell 1.7%. On the positive side, America Movil edged up 0.3% after Starlink’s decision to position itself as a direct rival to traditional telecoms rather than a low-cost disruptor eased some competitive fears. What matters today. Wednesday’s US CPI print will dictate whether the peso and the IPC regain their footing or test the bottom of their summer trading ranges.

01 The session in one read

Mexico’s equity market started the week on the back foot, with the S&P/BMV IPC — the benchmark that tracks the 35 largest and most liquid companies listed in Mexico — dropping 0.75% to settle at 66,439 points. The decline was choreographed not by a single panic, but by a series of sharp, targeted sell-offs in names sensitive to consumer spending and infrastructure travel.

The peso largely sat out the drama. The dollar bought 17.14 pesos by the close, a shift of barely 0.04% on the day, even as the US Dollar Index — a gauge of the greenback’s strength against six major currencies — ticked up 0.21% to 99.75.

The tone was cautious globally. The S&P 500 shed a marginal 0.06% and the technology-heavy Nasdaq fell 0.32%, while the VIX fear gauge popped 3.76% to 15.46. Traders across the Americas chose to lighten positions ahead of Wednesday’s US consumer-price report, the most consequential data point for interest-rate expectations this month.

Domestically, the market digested a blunt assessment from Banco de México (Banxico): the central bank’s governor noted officials are ‘not yet declaring victory’ over inflation, reinforcing the view that Mexico’s benchmark rate will stay elevated for longer. That backdrop makes any dip in defensive, high-dividend names a potential buying opportunity for local pension funds.

Assessment — Risk-Off, but Orderly MEDIUM Monday’s decline was broad but not panicked. The VIX rose 3.76%, indicating some nerves on Wall Street, yet Mexican volume leaders were heavily weighted toward defensive names. The earthquake in Colombia injected an unusual geopolitical element, hurting airport stocks directly, but the macro trigger is undeniably Wednesday’s US inflation report. A lower CPI print could fuel bets that Banxico will resume its easing cycle later in the year; a hot number risks pushing the peso toward 17.50. The variable to watch is how the US 10-year yield — currently at 4.698% — reacts in the first hour after the data.

02 The day’s numbers

The IPC is now entrenched in the lower half of its annual range, having surrendered the 67,000 handle that briefly provided support in early August. At 66,439, the benchmark sits firmly below its falling 50-day moving average, a trend-following line that has acted as a ceiling for every relief rally over the past two months.

The peso remains remarkably stable. The USD/MXN pair is hugging the 17.14 mark, which is a full 8.5% below its 52-week high of 18.74, meaning the Mexican currency has strengthened considerably from its worst levels. That strength, however, is now being openly questioned by officials concerned about its competitive impact on exports.

03 Why it moved — retail rout, quake jitters, and pre-CPI caution

The heaviest weight on the IPC came from Walmex, the Mexican unit of Walmart and typically a defensive crown jewel. Its shares sank 2.9% on Monday, with just $14 million changing hands. The drop erased the tentative gains the stock had booked late last week, suggesting some institutional investors trimmed their exposure ahead of a US inflation print that could re-price consumer-sector expectations.

Airport operators were caught in a unique crossfire. Grupo Aeroportuario del Pacífico, known as GAP, slumped 3.2% — the steepest loss on the index — while Grupo Aeroportuario del Centro Norte, trading as OMA, lost 1.2%. The trigger was a devastating magnitude 7.4 earthquake that struck Colombia, killing at least 132 people and briefly disrupting airport operations in the region. Although the physical damage was concentrated in Colombia, Mexican airport groups with international portfolios reacted to the broader risk of travel disruption and potential uninsured losses.

On the other side of the ledger, telecom heavyweight America Movil edged up 0.3% on decent $28 million turnover. The lift came after Starlink’s operational shift — from a niche disruptor to a direct challenger for traditional telecom subscribers — was digested. Investors interpreted the move as a validation of existing network infrastructure, making America Movil’s dense Latin American grid appear harder to replicate than initially feared.

Mining names provided a mixed picture. Grupo Mexico slipped 0.3% in heavy $32 million volume, while silver producer Peñoles advanced 3.7%. The divergence tracked metal prices: gold rose 1.40% while silver surged 3.7%, rewarding the more silver-focused portfolio of Peñoles.

The most-traded stock was Banorte, Mexico’s largest domestically controlled bank, which fell 1.3% on meaty $51 million volume. The decline reflects a broader rotation out of yield-sensitive financials ahead of the US CPI; traders worry that sticky inflation in the US will delay Fed easing and keep Banxico from cutting rates, capping loan growth expectations.

The gainers list was led by Vista Energy, an Argentina-focused oil-and-gas producer whose Mexican listing rose 4.1%. That move was partly a catch-up play and partly a currency-hedge trade, driven by Argentine energy deregulation hopes rather than a Mexico-specific catalyst. Among genuinely local names, broadcaster Televisa added 2%, rebounding from deeply oversold levels after weeks of steady selling.

05 The regional scoreboard

Latin American markets split in two directions on Monday. The Colombian Colcap climbed 0.94%, showing remarkable resilience despite the devastating earthquake, as emergency aid announcements — including $15.5 million from the US — and reconstruction-linked buying supported cement and construction shares. Argentina’s Merval surged 1.14%, extending its gravity-defying rally as local investors continued to pile into equities as a shield against still-high inflation.

Brazil’s Ibovespa edged down 0.19%, mirroring the cautious global tone, while Chile’s IPSA inched up 0.11%. World.title: Two men injured after licensed gun owner fires warning shots during San Pedro altercation
World.content:
Two men injured after licensed gun owner fires warning shots during San Pedro altercation

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a shooting incident in San Pedro Town after two young men reported sustaining gunshot injuries during an altercation involving several persons early Sunday morning.

Police responded to Lion Street at approximately 1:45 a.m. on August 9, where they spoke with 29-year-old mechanic Francisco Daniel Nah.

According to police, Nah reported that he was at a store when two golf carts arrived and their male occupants became involved in a verbal altercation, during which bottles were thrown.

Nah told investigators that one of the men approached him and reached toward his waist, leading him to believe that the man was retrieving a firearm. Fearing for his life, Nah, who police say is licensed to carry a 9mm pistol, fired three warning shots into the ground.

The occupants of the golf carts subsequently left the area.

However, at approximately 1:30 p.m. later that day, 20-year-old Rennel Aguilar and 19-year-old Edwin Barco reported to police that they had sustained gunshot injuries during the incident. Both men were taken for medical treatment.

Police have not indicated whether investigators have established what caused the men’s injuries or whether they were struck by rounds fired from Nah’s licensed weapon.

The investigation continues.

World.title: Two 19-year-olds hospitalized following Dangriga shooting
World.content:
Two 19-year-olds hospitalized following Dangriga shooting

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police are investigating a shooting in Dangriga Town that left two 19-year-old men hospitalized on Saturday night.

Police say that at approximately 8:30 p.m. on August 8, officers visited the Southern Regional Hospital after receiving reports of a shooting and found Kevon Higinio and Jim Mendez, both of Dangriga, suffering from apparent gunshot wounds.

Initial investigations indicate that Higinio had just left an establishment when he was approached by two male persons who opened fire in their direction, injuring both Higinio and Mendez.

Both men were listed in stable condition and remained hospitalized under observation.

Police investigations into the shooting continue. The incident and identities of the two injured men have also been reported by local media.

World.title: Post-mortem confirms Samuel Chi died from drowning; police investigation continues
World.content:
Post-mortem confirms Samuel Chi died from drowning; police investigation continues

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police say a post-mortem examination conducted on fisherman Samuel Chi has determined his cause of death to be asphyxia due to drowning, while toxicology results remain pending.

Chi disappeared at sea along with Albert Vaccaro after the men went on a fishing trip on Sunday, August 2 and failed to return as expected.

A joint search involving the Belize Coast Guard and other authorities was launched, and Vaccaro was found alive the following day floating in waters southwest of Hicks Caye. Authorities said at the time that he was dehydrated and disoriented and was unable to provide a clear account of what had occurred.

Chi remained missing until his body was recovered the following morning in waters west of Hicks Caye.

During Monday’s police press briefing, authorities said the forensic pathologist found the cause of death to be asphyxia due to drowning. Police indicated that the post-mortem did not establish evidence of violence.

However, investigators are still trying to determine the circumstances that led to Chi and Vaccaro ending up in the water.

Police could not confirm during the briefing whether investigators have since obtained a comprehensive statement from Vaccaro, noting that he was initially too disoriented to provide investigators with much information.

Chi’s family has publicly raised questions about the circumstances surrounding his death and expressed suspicions that foul play may have been involved.

Police say the investigation remains ongoing.

World.title: Belize City man charged in connection with Faber’s Road shooting
World.content:
Belize City man charged in connection with Faber’s Road shooting

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have arrested and charged a 26-year-old Belize City man in connection with a shooting incident in the Faber’s Road area over the weekend.

Gregory Williams has been charged with abetment to commit aggravated assault following a police investigation into the incident, which occurred at approximately 7:00 p.m. on Saturday, August 8.

According to police, a man reported that he was at his residence when a motorcycle carrying two men approached him.

One of the men aboard the motorcycle allegedly fired a single shot in his direction.

Police subsequently arrested Williams in connection with the incident.

Authorities say another individual is being sought as part of the ongoing investigation.

World.title: Punta Gorda man charged with drug trafficking after police seize 17.63 grams of crack cocaine
World.content:
Punta Gorda man charged with drug trafficking after police seize 17.63 grams of crack cocaine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have arrested and charged a 59-year-old Punta Gorda resident following the discovery of two quantities of suspected crack cocaine at his home.

Mark Lopez has been charged with two counts of possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply to another person.

Police say officers executed a search warrant at Lopez’s residence on Friday, August 7, during which they allegedly discovered two separate quantities of suspected crack cocaine.

The drugs reportedly weighed 10.97 grams and 6.66 grams respectively, for a combined weight of 17.63 grams.

Lopez was subsequently detained and formally charged.

World.title: Santa Elena man charged after police allegedly find 5.9 grams of cocaine
World.content:
Santa Elena man charged after police allegedly find 5.9 grams of cocaine

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Police have arrested and charged a 24-year-old Santa Elena resident after he was allegedly found in possession of suspected cocaine over the weekend.

Christopher Bolon has been charged with possession of controlled drugs with intent to supply.

Police say the arrest followed an operation conducted by Santa Elena police shortly before 1:00 a.m. on Saturday, August 8.

During the operation, officers allegedly found Bolon in possession of 5.9 grams of suspected cocaine.

He was subsequently detained and formally charged.

World.title: Three killed in Mahogany Street motorcycle collision
World.content:
Three killed in Mahogany Street motorcycle collision

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Three men have died following a collision involving two motorcycles on Mahogany Street in Belize City early Sunday morning.

Police say that at approximately 12:26 a.m. on August 9, officers responded to the area near the intersection of Mahogany and Tibruce Streets, where they found two extensively damaged motorcycles.

The victims were identified as Darwin Monroy, Allan Arnold and 22-year-old Theodore Swaso, all of Belize City.

According to police, Arnold was travelling on a motorcycle in one direction while Monroy was travelling in the opposite direction with Swaso as his pillion rider when the two motorcycles collided.

All three men sustained grave injuries. Arnold and Monroy died shortly after the collision, while Swaso was rushed to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital, where he later succumbed to his injuries.

Police say only one motorcycle helmet was recovered from the scene. Investigators have not yet established who was wearing the helmet at the time of the collision.

The circumstances surrounding the fatal crash remain under investigation.

World.title: Mundialito opening season 2026 kicks off
World.content:
Mundialito opening season 2026 kicks off

By Zoila Palma: The Mundialito Opening Season 2026 officially kicked off on August 8 at Berger Field, bringing together young footballers from across Belize to compete in several youth categories.

The tournament features the U-13 and U-10 male categories as well as the U-15 female category, providing an opportunity for Belize’s young players to showcase their skills and develop their talent.

The competition continues on August 11 at Berger Field, with the next game scheduled for 2:00 p.m. Football fans are encouraged to come out and support the young athletes as they compete for top honors.

World.title: Tougher water fines
World.content:
Water level in the Mona reservoir last week.

SEVEN parishes will face a water prohibition from Monday, August 17 as the Government moves to tighten restrictions amid worsening drought conditions.

At the same time, Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda is set to approach the executive and legislature to punish violators with stiffer fines.

“As we had to do after the first incident that took place with Rio Cobre, where we had to shift the fine, we now have to take the same approach with fines in relation to water prohibition,” Samuda told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

“Because of the present forecast and warning associated with El Niño, we will have to move with unprecedented speed, and we will have to engage first the Cabinet and then Parliament in the coming weeks to facilitate this,” Samuda added.

On Monday, Samuda’s ministry, through the National Water Commission (NWC), announced that the water prohibition orders will apply to Kingston, St Andrew, St Thomas, St Mary, Portland, St Ann, and St Catherine and will remain in force until further notice.

“Under the orders, no person shall use or cause water supplied by the NWC to be used for non-essential or unusual purposes. Prohibited activities include:

• irrigation or watering of gardens, lawns, grounds, and farms;

• refilling or supplying of ponds or swimming pools and/or for use other than normal domestic services such as drinking, cooking, washing, bathing, and sanitation;

• washing of vehicles by the use of a hose;

• watering or washing of roadways, pavements, paths, garages, or out-rooms;

• any activity requiring excessive or unusual quantities of water,” the ministry release stated.

The ministry said the decision followed a high-level stakeholder meeting earlier Monday with the NWC and the Meteorological Service, which confirmed that rainfall levels remain critically low and temperatures continue to soar.

Underscoring the necessity of the measure, Samuda said, “We understand that there is some disproportionate economic impact on commercial operations, such as car washes, and we have not taken this decision lightly. Ultimately, our priority is to maintain supply to critical services, especially schools, as we prepare for the September reopening.”

He further advised that sanctions will be applied to individuals and entities found in breach of the prohibition order, noting “these penalties are intended to ensure compliance and protect the integrity of Jamaica’s water supply during this critical period”.

The current fine for breaching an NWC prohibition order is $1,000. Failure to pay the court-ordered fine results in imprisonment for up to 30 days.

Samuda’s reference to the Rio Cobre was the action taken by the Government after chemical spills that resulted in fish kills that affected several species and impacted other aquatic organisms four years ago.

In January 2025 he successfully piloted a Bill in the House of Representatives which approved amendments to the Natural Resources Conservation Authority (NRCA) Act and the Wild Life Protection Act to allow for significant increases in fines and related custodial sentences.

Under the Acts, depending on the severity of the offence, as adjudicated by the Supreme Court, corporate bodies may now be subject to a fine of approximately $10 million, individuals in breach of the Acts may face a fine of up to $5 million or serve a term of imprisonment up to five years, subject to the jurisdiction of the parish courts.

On Monday, Samuda told the Observer that the request he will be taking to Cabinet and Parliament is to “move the fines in line with what was done for bodies corporate and individuals under the NRCA Act breaches.

The naturally-occurring El Niño climate pattern, which began in June and is expected to peak later this year, has already amplified unprecedented temperatures across the world.

Some 33 countries recorded their hottest July since records began, according to a detailed analysis of billions of data points from Copernicus’s ERA5 climate model.

The severe drought has triggered food security concerns worldwide.

Last week, the United Nations World Food Programme said that Central America is expected to be the region hardest hit in terms of the relative increase in food insecurity.

Including the Caribbean, the agency estimates that an additional 16 million people could face food insecurity by the end of 2027.

World.title: Who hurt the child?
World.content:
AN announcement by the Child Protection and Family Services Agency (CPFSA) that it is fast-tracking the installation of security cameras at Glenhope Place of Safety, even as it probes the injuries suffered by a one-year-old boy who had been in its care, has been welcomed by attorney Denise Hinson who is adamant that somebody needs to be held accountable for how the child came to be injured in such a manner.

“The questions still need to be answered. This should not be pushed under the rug. I’m angry, and I think that someone needs to explain why a one-year-old defenceless child, a Jamaican child, looks as if he was in an MMA (mixed martial arts) fight,” Hinson told the Jamaica Observer on Monday.

The attorney is representing the mother of the child who is before the court for immigration issues.

She said the child’s injuries captivated the attention of the St Catherine Parish Court last Friday when the matter was called up before Justice Roneiph Lawrence.

Hinson said the child’s Haitian mother, Fabienne Cherisma, who was recently arrested for overstaying her visa alongside her husband who is said to have used fraudulent documents to obtain Jamaican citizenship, were on Friday brought before the court so it could make a further order for the child to remain in the custody of the State.

However, Hinson said when the child was presented to the court, both parents went into shock.

“The child was taken to court with [healing] black and blue bruises under both eyes; what seemed to be burn marks to the right cheek and chin; swelling of the face, especially to the right cheek; and scratches to the nose. Both eyes were bloodshot in the corners. A medical shown to the court by the CPFSA officer who brought the baby to court, described the injuries as ‘non-accidental’,” Hinson told the Observer.

The attorney said that when the mother saw her child she “screamed and began to cry uncontrollably and the father collapsed. They had to be removed and later returned to the dock”.

Hinson said the court was also “visibly disturbed by the doctor’s findings and the injuries on the baby’s face”.

She said the CPFSA officer, when pressed by the judge about the cause of the child’s injuries, “informed the court that when she asked, on arriving to collect the child, she was told that he had hit his face on the crib”.

The attorney, in making a successful bail application on behalf of the mother, who was released on humanitarian grounds, however countered that, “both eyes were bruised and that could not have occurred if the child simply fell out his crib”.

“I also pointed out that the child is in danger where he is and that he needed his mother. My focus is really to get to the bottom of how the child received those injuries at Glenhope. Also, the bruises were healing and the burn mark almost completely healed. However, the child didn’t see a doctor until the day before court, on August 6, 2026. I need help in finding out when and how the child was injured and why the child wasn’t taken to the doctor until the day before the scheduled court date,” Hinson declared.

The attorney said she is in discussion with the child’s mother to determine the legal options available to her as she presses for answers regarding her son’s health. Hinson told the Observer that her client is adamant that the “child was in perfect health when removed from [their] home”.

The CPFSA issued a statement to the media on Monday saying “the incident is being investigated and is being treated with utmost urgency and importance”.

The agency stated that it “takes a zero-tolerance approach to all forms of child abuse” and said, based on the outcome of the investigation, it stands ready to execute all measures or sanctions regarding child abuse, in keeping with the Child Care and Protection Act (CCPA 2004).

Furthermore, the CPFSA said under its 2025–2027 strategic framework it established an islandwide initiative to equip residential child care facilities with security cameras, ensuring high safety standards are maintained across all locations.

“In light of the recent incident however, deployment has been prioritised to fast-track installation at the facility in which this incident has taken place,” the agency pledged.

World.title: Wellington praises Team Jamaica after World U-20 exploits
World.content:
Shanoya Douglas won three medals for Jamaica — gold in the women’s 4x100m relay and silver in the 100m and 200m. (Photo: Paul Reid)

OREGON, USA — Keith Wellington, team leader for Jamaica at the 21st staging of the World Athletics Under-20 Championships, says the team performed well despite the challenges of a long season.

Jamaica won eight medals — two gold, three silver and three bronze — to finish fourth on the medal table and third in the placing table with 89 points.

Hosts United States topped both tables with 24 medals —12 gold, seven silver and five bronze. Kenya were second with 11 medals — four gold, three silver and four bronze — while Italy finished third with five medals — three gold and two bronze.

Shanoya Douglas was Jamaica’s most successful athlete, winning three medals — gold in the women’s 4x100m relay and silver in the 100m and 200m.

Wellington said the performances were particularly impressive given that most of the athletes had been competing since January.

“I think under any circumstances this would be a really good performance,” Wellington told the Jamaica Observer on Sunday before the final two relays were contested. “Eight medals to date, and third in terms of quality.”

He said the overall standard at the championships had improved significantly.

“We have seen some really world-class standards, not just as juniors but the quality of the performances has been really, really good overall for all the countries. And so, to still be amongst the best, I think, we would be proud of the performances.”

Wellington singled out Michael Andre Edwards’ dramatic victory in the men’s triple jump during which he produced a World Under-20-leading and personal best 17.08m — the fifth-longest winning mark in the history of the event at the championships.

“Yeah, I think the obvious standout would be Team Captain Michael Andre’s performance. Not just the 17.08m but remember, you know, he took the lead with his second-to-last jump. It was taken away from him and he came back and claimed it. So it’s not just the result, but the quality and the performance there.”

He also highlighted the men’s discus throw competition on Sunday involving Jamaicans Joseph Salmon and Kamari Kennedy, when the lead changed several times over the final two rounds.

Jamaica also set two national records in the mixed 4x100m relay, which was contested for the first time at the championships, and the mixed 4x400m relay.

Ten Jamaicans produced personal bests, including Shevaughn Thomas and Sashane Johnson who each recorded two personal best performances.

Wellington said the athletes’ performances should not be judged solely by their results, pointing to the demands of the Jamaican school season.

“I think we don’t want to just look at the results, but look at the performances and you can see quite a few quality performances. And we cannot ignore, again, that our juniors have a really long season; and it is the schools that invest most in these kids, so they have to peak for champs because that is where the investment is,” he said.

“And so, for them to come back five months after their last performance for their schools again is sometimes a challenge that many of them have exams in the middle and all of that. So, I think it’s an incredible performance.”

World.title: STAYING PUT!
World.content:
Sanjay Seymore (left) anchors Jamaica’s men’s 4x100m relay team to victory in the semi-finals of the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon, on Saturday. Jamaica ran 39.51 seconds to advance to the final. At centre is Hong Kong’s Cheuk Fung Jasper Koo, while at right is Australia’s Joshua John. (Photo: Paul A Reid)

OREGON, USA — William Knibb Memorial High School’s Sanjay Seymore has turned down several offers from United States colleges, choosing to remain in Jamaica as he targets places on the country’s teams for the 2027 World Athletics Championships and 2028 Olympic Games.

The ISSA/GraceKennedy Boys’ and Girls’ Athletics Championships and Carifta Games 200m champion is coming off a season of highs and lows, including finishing third in his favourite event at the Jamaica Athletics Administrative Association (JAAA) National Junior Championships and missing out on an individual spot on Jamaica’s team to the 21st World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon.

Seymore, who recently signed a professional contract, declined to give details about his plans but confirmed to the Jamaica Observer on Sunday that he would remain in Jamaica for now.

“I can say definitely I’m staying in Jamaica for now. So yes, that’s the only thing I can say right now that I would be staying in Jamaica.”

He said he believes remaining at home gives him the best opportunity to make Jamaica’s teams for the World Championships and Olympics.

“It’s just I think it’s the best for me right now, I don’t really have anything against college,” he said. “I see that when you go college and then come back for the Jamaica trials, athletes are not at their best and then and you know we have World Championship and Olympics coming up.”

At 19, Seymore believes he has time to develop as he prepares to compete against some of the world’s leading sprinters, including Jamaica’s Oblique Seville.

“They already have their reputations, Oblique Seville is a world champion, so you can’t take that from him. So, as the rookie, I would say I’m just going into the big game with the seniors, and I’m just going to give it my best shot always, like I done in junior levels. But I know I have to put the best foot forward if I want to make it big as a Jamaican sprinter. So that’s definitely goal for me.”

Seymore had been expected to qualify for Jamaica’s team in the 200m but suffered an injury shortly before the JAAA Championships. He finished third in the final in 21.01 seconds behind Nathaniel Martin and Kyle Bodden.

He was subsequently added to the men’s 4x100m relay team and ran two strong anchor legs as Jamaica won bronze.

“After Carifta I had some injuries, went to trials and came third as I was coming back from the injury,” he said. “But I got my mind right and told myself I’m going to go on this relay and I’m going to give it my best shot and go into the best possible shape I can for the team.”

Seymore said he was pleased with his contribution to the bronze-medal effort.

“So I just went out there and give my best and we came short of the gold medal, but we still made the podium, so I’m pretty happy for that.”

World.title: BWE organisers respond to viral fight video, reaffirms commitment to patron safety
World.content:
Videograb showing a brawl at a Best Weekend Ever beach event on Sunday, August 10, 2026.

ST ANN, Jamaica – The directors of party series Best Weekend Ever (BWE) has expressed disappointment and regret over a physical altercation involving patrons at its beach event on Sunday.

Videos of the incident have been widely circulated on social media, showing a group of men engaged in a brawl.

In a media release Monday, the party organisers said, “Best Weekend Ever has never condoned, and we abhor the proliferation of violence of any kind at our events.

“We are extremely disappointed and sincerely regret that this unfortunate and isolated situation has occurred,” the release continued. “We have contacted the family of those affected and the individuals involved in the altercation have been clearly identified, and the relevant actions will be pursued by the designated authority.”

According to the directors, over the years, BWE has established a strong track record of providing safe, well-managed entertainment experiences for thousands of patrons.

“The safety and security of our guests remain a priority, and this incident is not reflective of the culture of Best Weekend Ever or the experience we work diligently to provide,” they said.

The directors also sought to clarify that, contrary to some narratives circulating, the MC at the event “brought attention to the incident to allow the appropriate intervention to take place and we have made our team available to the relevant authorities to assist in the process of ensuring this does not reoccur.”

According to the release, throughout the staging of Best Weekend Ever 2026, the events have been enjoyed safely by thousands of patrons with improved traffic management and movement between events.

“We are also grateful for the positive feedback from patrons which is an indication of the high level of satisfaction with the production of the event series,” the organisers said.

“Additional security measures have been put in place for the final event being staged today,” they added. “We thank our patrons, partners, security teams and stakeholders for their support as we continue to remain committed to delivering an environment where everyone can celebrate responsibly and safely.”

World.title: Tropical depression could form in Atlantic by the end of the week
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — The United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is advising that a tropical depression could form in the Atlantic during the latter half of this week.

The NOAA says an area of low pressure located a few hundred miles south of the Cabo Verde Islands is producing disorganised showers and thunderstorms.

As this system moves slowly westward, a tropical wave currently over west Africa is expected to merge with it in a couple of days.

Environmental conditions are forecast to be more conducive for development by midweek, and a tropical depression could form during the latter half of this week while the system moves westward to west-northwestward across the central tropical Atlantic.

Formation chance through 48 hours is low at 20 per cent but formation chance through seven days is medium at 60 per cent.

World.title: Bold Bruce
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Bruce Golding

NEW YORK, USA — Former Jamaican Prime Minister Bruce Golding has earned the backing of many within the Diaspora community here for what is being described as his “bold, factual and truthful position” on the souring relationship between Jamaica and America, two staunch allies.



Speaking in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania last week, Golding expressed hopes that “the United States will soften the tone of its relationship with Jamaica and rekindle the strong, decades-old bond between both nations which Jamaicans cherish.

Saying that current demands by Washington are “at odds with the very essence of true friendship”, he pointed to the many challenges facing the island as established rules are being discarded and “new rules are being handed down, not after discussions and negotiations, but unilaterally by social media postings at 2:30 in the morning when most of us are asleep”.

The former Jamaican leader, who stepped away in 2011 and handed over the reins to now Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness, was addressing the annual Team Jamaica Bickle Independence Gala on Emancipation Day, August 1, 2026.

The gala celebrated Jamaica’s 64th anniversary of Independence and raised funds in support of Jamaican and other Caribbean athletes’ participation in the yearly Penn Relays in the US, a must-stop on the annual sports calendar for speedy Jamaican high school students.

Golding appeared to be voicing sentiments many Jamaicans in his US audience feel but could not express themselves. Some murmured among themselves that he must not fear losing his US visa.

Called to ask his view Sunday, Golding said he did not wish to trivialise the matter and he had said enough on the subject.

But reacting to the former prime minister’s assessment of the bilateral relations, Stafford Grant, founder and president of the US-based Jamaica Ex-Service Men and Women Foundation, said after the speech:

“Golding didn’t just give a speech, he gave Jamaica a masterclass in geopolitical survival. His address laid bare the brutal reality of being a small island nation caught in the cross hairs of superpower diplomacy.

“The former prime minister’s speech should serve as a profound wake-up call for every Jamaican. His vocal defence is more critical than ever, and I trust Jamaicans will understand that international diplomacy is shifting from collaborative negotiations to unilateral madness,” Grant declared.

Raymond Rhoden, a Florida-based retired adjunct professor, described Golding’s stance as “bold, principled, factual and diplomatic”, adding that he believes Jamaica needs to stand up and take a principled position on the current situation.

Irwine Clare Sr, co-founder of Team Jamaica Bickle, said the issues raised by the former head of government were “pungent, timely, and well articulated on behalf of the voiceless and those who have avoided the conversation due to fear of reprisal or just being downright spineless”.

“This speech must also be placed in context, because clearly he [Golding] recognises the agonising situation that Caribbean leaders find themselves in, especially against the backdrop that they do not speak from a united perspective,” said Clare Sr.

In his address, which was punctuated by applause, Golding spoke of the discontinuation of the Cuban medical mission programme, America’s fierce opposition to China’s investments in Jamaica, and the highly controversial third-country nationals arrangements between the US and a number of Caribbean countries, as examples of actions that run counter to harmonious relations.

“True friends don’t abuse your friendship; they don’t make unreasonable demands of you. They should be there to help you. Holding a gun at your head and insisting that you must be reasonable and do things their way is not friendship,” Golding suggested.

“The United States has put us under severe stress, and that’s not what friends are for,” he said, pointing to the damage the Jamaican economy could suffer should Jamaica stand up and try to fight back.

“There are many at home and abroad who are outraged at what is taking place, who are incensed at what is being meted out to us, who are angry that we have not pushed back, that we haven’t stood up like President Lula da Silva of Brazil who declared that, ‘Brazil’s destiny is for Brazilians alone to determine — without foreign interference or otherwise.’ “

Noting that Brazil is large and provides a US$57-billion market for American exports, Golding warned that little Jamaica is not in that league, struggling to find markets for its own goods.

“With the US market accounting for half our total exports, if our exports to the US market were slapped with a 50 per cent tariff our manufacturing sector would fall apart and thousands of persons would lose their jobs,” said Golding.

Agreeing with Golding, Dr Rupert Francis, who heads the Jamaica Diaspora Task Force on Crime Intervention and Prevention, argued that “we need to get back to the more amiable friendship we had with the United States for many years”.

University lecturer Dr Allan Cunningham said Golding’s speech focused on what he describes as the “hypocrisy of the rules-based order”, noting that “the speech acts as a call for regional realism — that without a unified foreign policy Caribbean states remain vulnerable to US cowboy diplomacy”.

World.title: Public funds not enough for climate resilience — Samuda
World.content:
Matthew Samuda, minister of water, environment and climate change, delivers the keynote address at National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited’s inaugural Corporate Insights Breakfast. Addressing business leaders, Samuda underscored the importance of public-private collaboration in strengthening Jamaica’s climate resilience and preparing businesses, communities and the wider economy for the growing risks associated with climate change..

MINISTER of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda is arguing that Jamaica cannot rely on public funds alone to build the infrastructure and systems needed to withstand the growing effects of climate change.

Samuda said greater participation will be required from private investors, financial institutions, and international partners as the country seeks to strengthen critical infrastructure and improve its ability to recover from climate-related disruptions.

“Public funds are simply not enough to address the challenges posed by climate change. We need financing from all available sources — including public, private, domestic and international partners — if we are to successfully transition to climate resilience,” Samuda said.

He was speaking at the inaugural NCB Corporate Breakfast Series, hosted by National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited (NCBJ), which brought together policymakers, business leaders and financial sector representatives to discuss climate resilience, infrastructure, and investment.

Samuda said strengthening Jamaica’s resilience will require cooperation across the public and private sectors as the country responds to the increasing threat posed by extreme weather and other climate-related events.

The issue has taken on greater significance as disruptions to electricity, water, telecommunications, transportation and other critical services can have wide-ranging effects on households, communities and businesses.

NCBJ Interim Chief Executive Officer Sheree Martin said the changing environment also requires organisations to rethink how they prepare for and respond to disruptions.

“Strategy sharpens in conversation, not in isolation, and capital works best when it is guided by an honest read on where a business is heading,” Martin said.

She said access to financing, strong partnerships, and informed decision-making will become increasingly important as organisations adjust to economic and structural changes.

“As businesses adapt to changing realities, access to informed perspectives, strong partnerships, and the right financial solutions become increasingly important,” Martin said.

Hugh Graham, director of Paramount Industries, said businesses also have a responsibility to prepare for disruptions and protect their operations and employees.

“For businesses, resilience is about being able to keep operating, protect jobs, and continue serving customers when disruption occurs,” Graham said.

“That requires investment and preparation at the company level, but it also requires strong infrastructure, sound policy,and access to financing.” Graham said closer coordination among Government, financial institutions, and businesses could improve Jamaica’s ability to withstand shocks and recover more quickly. “The more Government, financial institutions, and businesses can plan together, the better positioned we will be to withstand shocks and recover more quickly,” he said. NCB said the breakfast series is intended to bring together policymakers, business leaders, and other stakeholders to discuss issues affecting Jamaica’s economic development and long-term sustainability.

World.title: Putin used North Korean ballistic missiles in lethal attack on Ukraine, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean ruler Kim Jong Un have deepened ties since the Kremlin’s war on Ukraine began. In September last year during a meeting in Beijing, Kim vowed to do “everything we can to assist Russia.”

Zelenskyy also reported attacks on a Kyiv hospital and businesses overnight, with at least one person injured. The capital’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, urged residents late Monday to seek shelter.

Moscow also attacked substations in Kherson and Kharkiv, causing power outages, Zelenskyy said. Further attacks took place in the Donetsk, Dnipro and Mykolaiv regions.

“Every step Russia takes — increasing ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilization — all of this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation,” Zelenskyy wrote.

Russia has stepped up its missile attacks this summer, with Zelenskyy urging Western allies to help Kyiv strengthen its air defenses and to heap sanctions pressure on companies fueling Moscow’s war. However, Europe is running out of Patriot interceptors to shoot down Russian missiles, according to the continent’s military officials.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has struck back, targeting Russian infrastructure including oil refineries and buildings belonging to e-commerce giant Wildberries.

Russian state media on Tuesday reported that two Wildberries warehouses in the Voronezh region, several hundred kilometers south of Moscow, caught fire following drone strikes, killing one person.

World.title: Trump backs Infantino after fury over FIFA chief’s World Cup sale plan
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino and U.S. President Donald Trump with the World Cup trophy before presenting it to Spain after the final at New York New Jersey Stadium on July 19, 2026. | Dan Mullan/Getty Images

It would be a “terrible mistake” to replace the football boss after the success of the 2026 World Cup, the U.S. president posted on Truth Social.

U.S. President Donald Trump backed under-pressure football chief Gianni Infantino, after calls grew for the FIFA boss to quit following his aborted plan to sell off parts of the World Cup tournament to private investors.

“FIFA would be making a terrible mistake if, for any reason, they even considered replacing President Gianni Infantino. He is fantastic, having just presided over the most successful World Cup, by four times, ever presented,” Trump posted Tuesday morning on Truth Social.

Trump and Infantino cultivated a close relationship in the run-up to the 2026 World Cup, hosted this summer in North America, and the U.S. president helped present the trophy to victorious Spain in New Jersey in July.
