World.title: Germany’s modern miracle: Churches are losing believers but gaining money
World.content:
Rising salaries have outweighed the cost of hundreds of thousands leaving the church.

German commentators are calling it a modern-day “miracle.”

Hundreds of thousands of worshippers are walking away from their churches each year. The money, however, keeps rolling in.

Some 660,000 people formally quit the country’s Catholic and Protestant churches in 2025, freeing them from a levy automatically charged to registered members as a percentage of their income tax bill.

Despite the exodus, the two institutions collected more than €12.5 billion through the church tax for the 2025 fiscal year, up from around €12.4 billion in 2024.

The apparent miracle has a decidedly earthly explanation: Rising wages and Germany’s progressive tax system mean the shrinking pool of members is paying more.

“At first glance, the development may seem contradictory,” a spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany — the umbrella organization representing Germany’s regional Protestant churches — said. “The reason is that church tax is calculated based on individual income tax.”





Members of Germany’s Catholic and Protestant churches and some Jewish communities pay an additional religious tax equal to 8 or 9 percent of their income tax liability, even if they don’t attend services.

In 2021, the most recent year for which comprehensive data is available, more than 29 million people paid church tax in Germany, amounting to almost half of all income taxpayers in Europe’s largest economy.

The German Finance Ministry’s 2025 payroll tax tables suggests that a single employee without children earning €50,000 gross a year pays approximately €600 in church tax annually on top of income tax, depending on the federal state. Someone earning €70,000 per year pays more than €1,000.

People are registered as part of their religious community at birth or at local government offices. To stop paying the church tax, they must formally leave through a process known as Kirchenaustritt, or “church exit.”

The procedure varies across Germany’s federal states but typically requires appearing in person at a registry office or local court to submit a declaration. Most states also charge an administrative fee.

While those who deregister can still attend services as a visitor and access some church services, they are not allowed to have a church wedding, be a godparent or be guaranteed a church burial.

In 2025, some 310,000 left the Catholic Church, while around 350,000 left one of Germany’s regional Protestant churches.

Church exit

The reasons people give for formally leaving their religious communities range from feeling less connected to the church to simply wanting to save money.

“People are leaving the Church because they feel it no longer plays a role in their lives,” said Matthias Kopp, director of communications for the German Bishops’ Conference.

“Added to this are the scandals of recent years, which have called the Church’s credibility into question,” he added. “There are also people — though this is by no means the primary reason — who leave the Church because of the church tax.”

“These are processes of alienation to which we must respond,” said Kopp.

For Jana Keil, a 33-year-old accountant from Berlin, the decision was both financial and moral. “I no longer wanted to support the system with church tax in light of the [child sex] abuse scandals,” she said.





Lukas Heinich, a 23-year-old working student, said he formally left after completing his apprenticeship because he “didn’t feel like paying the tax or supporting the church.”

That church tax revenues continue to rise despite the exodus is down to the types of taxpayers choosing to remain church members.

Those who are still paying church tax in Germany are “probably the higher earners,” said Zareh Asatryan, professor of empirical economics at the University of Münster. “Those that stay will naturally earn more income because of inflation plus real wage growth, and they will just generate more revenue.”

A miracle with an end date?

But the continued rise in church tax revenue masks significant long-term challenges — and raises questions about how long the trend can last.

While those revenues are going up, they are “relatively sluggish” and “haven’t been increasing by a lot,” said Asatryan.

The increase in revenue from the church tax is considerably lower than the increase in revenue from income tax. State revenue from wage and income taxes rose by 6.65 percent in 2025, said Kopp, whereas church tax revenue increased by 1.93 percent.

“Long-term projections indicate that church tax revenue will decline significantly over the coming decades as church membership continues to decrease,” said the spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany.

Protestant churches are already preparing for their income to decrease “through long-term planning processes,” said the spokesperson. “Without this system, the church’s religious, social and charitable work would not be possible on its current scale.”

World.title: EU opens channel with Meta, TikTok to tackle Ceuta migrant crisis
World.content:
That will serve as a point of contact for platforms, fact-checkers and the Commission to quickly flag content so that it can be reviewed and taken down if necessary. The effort comes amid concerns that disinformation is promoting further crossings into the territory on Aug. 15, according to Maldita.es. Maldita.es and the European Fact-Checking Standards Network attended Monday’s meeting.

The Commission operates a rapid response system under its code of conduct on disinformation, often triggered around elections. The new mechanism on Ceuta would bring a closer group of stakeholders together, two of the people said.

Another meeting has been set for later this week, one of those people and the third person confirmed.

Meta and TikTok said they were already actively monitoring the situation in line with their policies and had set up dedicated teams to monitor and respond to content in real time.

The crisis has divided EU countries and has reignited Europe’s long-running debate on illegal migration. Italy has since been one of the harshest critics of Spain’s left-wing government and its migration policies, and has implemented border controls for travelers arriving from Spain.

Former EU commissioner Thierry Breton, who was a force behind the EU’s online content rules, on Monday said the bloc should launch a disinformation inquiry into the Ceuta crisis in an interview with Italian newspaper La Stampa.

World.title: Greece’s aging power grid blamed for catastrophic wildfires
World.content:
Two deadly wildfires in late July — one in western Attica and one on the island of Crete —were also linked to the electricity grid in preliminary findings from the Greek fire brigade. The fires destroyed more than 36,000 acres and killed four people.

“Six out of 10 major fires and 55 percent of the area burnt in 2025 were caused by the power grid,” said Elias Tziritis, wildfires actions coordinator at World Wildlife Fund Greece. “Statistically speaking, the majority of fires may not start from the power grid, but these are the ones that cause the most major, devastating fires.”

Loose or sagging power lines, vegetation coming in contact with cables, dust buildup on transmission equipment and other such faults can all generate sparks. The risk rises during strong winds and periods of heavy electricity demand, when aging infrastructure is under greater strain.

Much of Greece’s electricity grid was installed decades ago and runs above ground through fire-prone forests and increasingly depopulated rural areas. In the 1960s, the country opted for an overhead network as a cheaper way to extend electricity across the country, while the prolonged financial crisis that began in 2009 further constrained investment in the system.

Critics say Greece has moved too slowly to bury distribution lines and adapt the network to increasingly severe fire conditions.

“We raised the issue years ago, calling for something to be done with the power grid urgently,” said Christos Kalogeropoulos, a retired lieutenant-general with the Fire Service and former director of the Arson Crimes unit. “We have been calling for urgent underground cabling.”

However, with the arrival of the first GLP-1 pill Wegovy (semaglutide) from Danish competitor Novo Nordisk — which launched in the U.S. and U.K. this year and is soon expected in some EU countries — demand for the more-convenient tablet is expected to rise.

World.title: Europe’s scorching summer is erasing its economic growth, says report
World.content:
The biggest drag is expected to come from people struggling to work in extreme heat. Triodos estimates lost labor productivity alone could shave around 0.6 percent off EU GDP, while agricultural output could fall by between 3 and 7 percent.

“At first sight this might seem modest, but it is exactly the expected economic growth for the EU this year,” said the bank of the overall €180 billion blow.

And the summer is not over. France and Britain are bracing for their fifth heat wave of the season this week, with temperatures nearing 40 degrees Celsius in southeastern France and 36 degrees forecast in the U.K.

The bill is already mounting beyond GDP. POLITICO estimated at least 14,000 excess deaths across the six hardest-hit European countries during the record-breaking heat wave from mid-June to early July.

Drought has also hammered Europe’s energy system: Low water levels in the Danube in recent weeks have forced sharp cuts at Hungary’s Paks nuclear plant and pushed Romania to blast apart a rock to divert water toward its last operating reactor. Vessels on the Rhine and Danube have had to sail only partially loaded.

In Austria, meanwhile, drought has caused an estimated €1 billion in agricultural losses, according to Austrian Hail Insurance, after some regions received more than 75 percent less rain than normal since mid-June.

Triodos warned against treating this summer as a freak event, saying extreme heat “might become structural” as the planet warms. But governments can soften the damage through irrigation, insulation, cooling and shifting working hours, said the bank.

“Every year adaptation without mitigation is a year borrowed against a hotter baseline.”

World.title: Iran executes woman who claimed self-defence against sexual assault
World.content:
Iran executed a young woman at dawn on Saturday who said she had acted in self-defence against a sexual assault, as authorities simultaneously handed a second woman ten death sentences in a separate case involving the killing of elderly men she had married.

 

Marzieh Nieri, 23, was executed at Qazvin Central Prison. Iran Human Rights said she had been forced into marriage at 17 under family pressure.

The incident that led to her execution occurred in October 2021, when she was 18.

At her trial, Nieri said one of her husband's business partners had attempted to assault her after becoming inebriated and that she wounded him with a kitchen knife in self-defence. Her husband was also killed during the confrontation.

Nieri turned herself in to the police four days after the incident, after going to her brother's home.

The court rejected her self-defence claim and, following a request from the victims' families for qisas — retribution in kind under the Islamic Republic's law — sentenced her to death.

Iran Human Rights said her execution brought the number of women executed in Iran since the start of 2026 to at least 14.

The executions come against a backdrop of sharply rising execution rates for women in Iran. The US State Department said at least 61 women were executed in Iran in 2025 — the highest figure in 25 years and roughly 70% more than the previous year. It described Iran as far ahead of any other country in the number of death sentences carried out against women.

Killing a husband or partner is one of the most common charges in cases involving women on death row in Iran. Iran Human Rights said at least 21 of the women executed in 2025 had been sentenced to qisas for killing their husbands or fiancés.

Women's rights organisations say many of those women had a history of domestic violence before the killing, and that forced marriage at a young age, economic dependence, restricted access to divorce and limited legal protection leave many women with few options for escaping abusive relationships.

Qisas is a principle in Iranian law derived from Islamic jurisprudence under which the family of a murder victim has the right to demand execution of the convicted killer, or to accept financial compensation — known as diyya, or "blood money" — in lieu of the death penalty.

Iranian courts can only carry out a death sentence in such cases with the explicit consent of the victim's next of kin.

Serial killer handed 10 death sentences

On the same day, the Mazandaran judiciary announced that Kolthoum Akbari had received 10 qisas death sentences for 10 killings.

The case against her opened in September 2023 after the suspicious death of an 82-year-old man in Mahmoudabad, who had died months after entering into a temporary marriage with Akbari.

His family's report to police led to an investigation that uncovered several other cases. Akbari confessed after her arrest to killing multiple elderly men, most of whom she had also married on a temporary basis. Her movable and immovable property was also confiscated.

The family of the 11th victim that Akbari was found guilty of murdering did not demand a death sentence in lieu of financial compensation. The authorities believe the total number of Akbari's victims is likely more than 11.

Iran is one of the few countries in the world that still applies the death penalty at scale. Human rights organisations recorded at least 1,639 executions in Iran in 2025 — the highest annual figure since 1989 and equivalent to more than four executions a day.

Amnesty International said only 17 countries carried out executions that year, with Iran second only to China.

Rights groups warn that executions have continued to rise in 2026, with the nationwide protests of December 2025 and the war with the US and Israel cited as factors increasing the risk of the death penalty being applied more broadly.

Amnesty International opposes the death penalty in all cases regardless of the crime or circumstances, describing it as a violation of the right to life.

World.title: Ithaca expects tourism surge after the release of Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey blockbuster
World.content:
Ithaca, in the Ionian Sea off the western coast of mainland Greece, lies far from the country’s popular tourist destinations and, despite its crystal-clear waters and spectacular coves, has never been one of travellers’ established hotspots.

 

That could soon be about to change thanks to the release of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, with fans of Homer and Odysseus adding Ithaca to their plans.

"I learned Greek when I was a child and I studied the Odyssey. I love Odysseus. This is my dream," says Italian lawyer Giorgia Ongarato, who arrived in Ithaca visibly moved.

Gidaki beach - Ithaca Φαίη Δουλγκέρη

The mayor of Ithaca expects that, after the Hollywood film, tourism will rise, but says the impact will only become clear next season.

"There still isn’t a large increase in visitors to the island because of the film. We think people will start planning from next year, as the film will gradually be released around the world. And that way everyone will start considering a trip to the island," Mayor Dionysis Stanitsas said.

On the other hand, there are business owners on Ithaca who have noticed that the island has already begun to gain global recognition following the film’s release.

"Tourists I have spoken to are already talking about it and say they believe something positive will come out of it. Although the film has not yet been released in all cinemas, it has already started to showcase the island and raise its profile thanks to its association with the movie," notes Xhimi Hotza.

Matt Damon, Christopher Nolan and Anne Hathaway AP Photo/Evan Agostini

Souvenir shop owners have long known the main reason tourists come to Ithaca, and it is none other than Homer and the Odyssey.

"People come because they know the legend of Odysseus and of Homer, who wrote the Odyssey. I think that is the main reason, but it is also a very beautiful, small island," says Ioanna Griva, a souvenir shop owner.

The permanent exhibition 'Light on Homeric Ithaca' in the village of Stavros presents archaeological finds that connect modern Ithaca with the homeland of Odysseus. Tegan Messing says, however, that the film does not have much in common with the original text: "I think it’s a good way to get more people interested in Homer and in mythology more generally. But the film certainly isn’t faithful to the original text."

Ithaca Φαίη Δουλγκέρη

Philologist and archaeologist Spyros Kouvaras is optimistic about tourism on Ithaca, but emphasises that it all comes down to Homer himself: "From next year we expect a significant increase in visitor numbers, and we can say that this will also affect the months that are usually dead. That is October, perhaps even November, as well as March and April, which are normally quiet months on Ithaca. And I would conclude by saying that behind this, first and foremost, is Nolan’s film, but behind Nolan’s film stands Homer."

World.title: Russia fired North Korean missiles in attack that killed six in Zaporizhzhia, Zelenskyy says
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Russia fired North Korean missiles in an overnight attack that killed six and wounded 19 in the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia.

 

"The city was struck with North Korean ballistic missiles, Zircons, and guided aerial bombs," he said, referring to Russia's hypersonic cruise missile system, Zircon.

Zelenskyy had warned on Monday evening that Russia was preparing to station more North Korean troops on its territory and had already received more ballistic missiles from Pyongyang.

He has repeatedly sounded the alarm over deepening military ties between Moscow and Pyongyang, often while appealing for more Western air-defence supplies.

"This is the first time they cannot wage war without supplements from North Korea," he said in his nightly address, referring to Russian forces.

"They are now preparing to deploy an additional contingent of Koreans on their territory. They have received, just imagine, additional ballistic missiles from North Korea," he added.

Only certain air defence systems, including US Patriots, are capable of intercepting ballistic missiles.

A shortage of PAC-3 interceptors has worsened since the war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in February.

At the same time, Ukraine has been increasing its strikes against Russian cities far from the border.

At the weekend, Zelenskyy said a decision had been taken for 30,000-50,000 North Koreans to be deployed on Russian soil. He did not explain how he obtained those figures.

North Korea has become one of Russia's closest military partners since Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed a mutual defence pact in June 2024.

Moscow used the North Korean troops in a counteroffensive later that year that pushed Ukrainian forces out of the border Kursk region.

Firefighters work to put out a fire after a Russian air strike on Zaporizhzhia, 11 August, 2026 @ZelenskyyUa

The overnight Russian attacks spanned Kyiv, Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk, regional authorities said.

Russia's defence ministry said its forces "delivered a group strike with high-precision ground-based weapons, hitting military-industrial enterprises and transport-logistics centres in the cities of Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia."

In Zaporizhzhia, Ivan Fedorov, head of the regional military administration, said Russian forces launched a "massive" attack using missiles and guided aerial bombs.

"Six people were killed and 19 others wounded," Fedorov wrote on Telegram, updating an earlier toll of five dead.

In the eastern Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian drone and artillery strikes on five districts killed three people and wounded five others, regional military administration head Oleksandr Ganzha said on Telegram.

Journalists in Kyiv said they heard a series of explosions shortly after midnight after authorities issued a missile alert.

Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on social media that the capital was "under ballistic missile attack."

Ukraine's emergency service said a warehouse caught fire and one person was wounded.

Kursk offensive

About 600 North Korean troops were killed fighting for Russia against Ukrainian forces, South Korea’s spy agency told lawmakers last year.

North Korea has suffered some 4,700 casualties, including injuries and deaths, the South Korean National Intelligence Service (NIS) told a parliamentary committee.

About 2,000 injured soldiers were repatriated to North Korea by air or train between January and March, according to the NIS.

Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks in Ulan-Ude, 10 August, 2026 AP Photo

The dead soldiers were cremated in Russia before their remains were sent back home, the intelligence agency said.

The assessment came after Pyongyang confirmed for the first time that it had sent troops to help Russia recapture parts of the Kursk region, which Ukraine took control of in a surprise incursion.

Meanwhile, North Korea's economy was showing signs of recovery as Pyongyang deepened trade and diplomatic ties with Russia and China, South Korea's unification ministry said in a report in April.

Rigid socialist planning and high military spending undermined growth in North Korea for years, as have sweeping international sanctions aimed at scuppering its development of nuclear weapons.

Soldiers march during the military parade marking the 80th anniversary of the founding of the ruling Worker's Party in Pyongyang, 10 October, 2025 AP Photo

China has long been the diplomatically isolated country's main economic backer, though Pyongyang has also drawn closer to Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Those relationships are now driving an improved economic outlook, with the North appearing to have "moved beyond a period of contraction" and "entered a phase of gradual recovery," according to the South Korean ministry.

Analysts said the North was also receiving economic and military technology assistance from Russia in return for sending troops and ammunition to help it fight Ukraine.

World.title: Why is the internet accusing Anne Hathaway of wearing a fake pregnancy belly?
World.content:
Everyone's talking about how Tom Holland and Zendaya are having a great year, but let's not forget that Anne Hathaway is making her mark on 2026.

 

The 43-year-old Oscar-winning actress has been one of the most bankable stars of the year, with roles in The Devil Wears Prada 2 and The Odyssey, and has also starred in one of our favourite films of the year so far – the underseen Mother Mary.

She's now on press tour duties for her latest role in David Robert Mitchell's The End Of Oak Street, a sci-fi survival film produced by J.J. Abrams - and therefore rumoured to be a part of his Cloverfield anthology universe.

As if that wasn't enough to celebrate, Hathaway is currently pregnant with her third child.

But because we can't have nice things, the internet went and made it weird.

We say weird, we mean idiotic - proving once again that deeply missed author Umberto Eco was right when he said that the tragedy of the internet "is that it has promoted the village idiot to the level of bearer of truth".

And a loud one at that.

Hathaway attended the world premiere of The End Of Oak Street at the Steven J. Ross Theater in Burbank in California, wearing a custom look by Atelier Prabal Gurung, consisting of low-rise jeans and a stylish crop top which showed off her baby bump.

Anne Hathaway at the premiere of The End of Oak Street on Sunday 9 August 2026 AP Photo

As per usual, Hathaway looked radiant, but certain social media users decided it was time to disprove Darwinism by accusing the actress of not only looking "bizarre" and "tacky" but wearing a fake pregnancy belly.

Following a viral post on X (where else?) from an account titled “21”, commenters pointed out that there was something "off" with Hathaway's stomach.

“Looks like a fake stomach. The belly button looks unreal,” one person commented. Another posted that it looked like "a prosthetic bump", while one user chimed in by writing: "As someone who has kids, her belly looks like those fake ones they use in movies."

Charming and not at all unwarranted.

The conspiracy theory went so viral that Hathaway was forced to respond, bringing classiness and humour to a pigsty.

She posted a video from the evening on Instagram and titled it: “Fake hair, real bump.”

Sadly - but somewhat predictably - that wasn't the end of it.

As if it wasn't distasteful enough to body shame and pass judgement on a pregnant woman's body, some commentators started blaming Hathaway's stylist for the apparently "unflattering wardrobe malfunction".

“Unflattering styling for a beautiful pregnant woman,” one wannabe fashionista wrote, while another commented: “Pregnancy is beautiful, but this is a stylist fail."

Now, to each their own when it comes to style and thoughts on low-rise jeans - but there are some crucial elements to take into consideration.

Firstly, why is this such a big deal?

Secondly, no two pregnancy bumps are identical. Grow up.

Thirdly, when you're carrying the weight of a person inside you, you should be able to wear whatever makes you happy and comfortable without fear of either judgement or baseless theories accusing you of faking your pregnancy. Like Demi Moore posing for Annie Leibovitz on Vanity Fair in 1991 and Rihanna proudly revealing her pregnancy during the Super Bowl Halftime Show in 2023, Hathaway isn't hiding her physical transformation and is choosing to celebrate it by not treating it as "unglamorous" or "weird", as certain folk on social media choose to label it. Their reaction smacks of still engrained stigma when it comes to maternity and women's changing bodies.

Then there's the wider context to think about.

Anne Hathaway is married to actor Adam Shulman and before having her first two children in 2016 and 2019, she experienced a miscarriage in 2015. Worse, she suffered her miscarriage while starring in the one-woman play, Grounded, in which she had to act out childbirth every night.

Hathaway has been open about this and recently spoke to late night host Seth Meyers about how shocked she was to have got pregnant so easily given her age and after fertility challenges.

Announcing her second pregnancy in 2019, she also shared the challenges of conception: “For everyone going through infertility and conception hell, please know it was not a straight line to either of my pregnancies. Sending you extra love.”

While it might still be too much to ask for the chronically online to embrace body positivity for all, maybe they could redirect all that energy towards more meaningful matters. Or stop depriving that village of their idiot.

Anne Hathaway stars in The End of Oak Street, which is out this week. Stay tuned to Euronews Culture for our full review.

World.title: Off sick for up to ten years: what lies behind Germany's teacher shortage
World.content:
Germany’s schools are facing a structural staffing crisis. More teachers have been hired and the federal states are trying to counter this by creating additional posts, recruiting lateral entrants and offering financial incentives.

 

Yet in many places there are still not enough staff to cover all lessons in full.

There is a particularly chronic shortage of teachers in the STEM subjects – mathematics, computer science, physics and chemistry. There is also a continuing nationwide or regional need in special needs education as well as in art and music.

According to the latest projection by the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education (KMK), there is a calculated shortfall of around 27,000 fully qualified teachers in Germany.

How dramatic the situation can become in individual regions is currently illustrated by Brandenburg. Education Minister Gordon Hoffmann (CDU) warned in June that the state would probably no longer be able to guarantee the standard timetable everywhere in the coming school year. The situation is particularly difficult in rural areas and in subjects such as biology and chemistry.

The situation also remains tense in North Rhine-Westphalia. Although the state now has more than 166,000 teaching posts, more than 7,770 positions were still unfilled most recently.

Berlin: Off sick for ten years

Berlin is an example of how sickness-related absences exacerbate the already strained staffing situation. According to the city’s education administration, 380 teachers have been on sick leave for at least a year. This emerges from a reply by the Senate to a parliamentary question from the MP Alexander King (BSW), first reported by the Berliner Morgenpost.

They include 225 civil servants and 155 salaried teachers. In total, Berlin employs around 35,000 teachers.

More specifically, 143 civil servant teachers have been absent for at least a year, and a further 50 for at least two years. According to the education administration, 18 teachers have even been on sick leave for at least ten years.

Primary schools are particularly hard hit, with 98 teachers out on long-term sick leave. Secondary schools are missing 54 teachers, grammar schools 34 and vocational schools 27.

There are also long-term absences among salaried teachers: five of them have been on sick leave for at least ten years, and 16 for at least five years.

The BSW MP Alexander King attributes this development, among other things, to the tight staffing situation: inadequate staffing levels increase the workload on those still in post and can in turn encourage further sickness-related absences.

North Rhine-Westphalia: sickness rate around 10 per cent

In Hesse, according to the Ministry of Education, around 225 of the approximately 67,000 teachers have been ill for at least a year, 16 of them for more than five years. Common causes cited include psychological strain and physical complaints.

In North Rhine-Westphalia, teachers in 2025 were on sick leave on average for 8.43 per cent of working days – more than in the state administration as a whole. Secondary modern schools (Hauptschulen) were particularly affected, with a sickness rate of 9.83 per cent.

In Saxony-Anhalt, around 8.6 per cent of lessons in the 2024/25 school year were cancelled because no cover could be provided.

It is impossible to say how many teachers nationwide have been off sick for at least a year. Why? The federal states collect and publish different sets of data. North Rhine-Westphalia, for example, distinguishes according to the duration of illness, while other states use other categories. The term "long-term illness" is also defined differently and in some states can apply to sick leave lasting more than 30 days.

Surveys in individual states nevertheless show that there are at least several hundred such cases.

The future: fewer teachers, more pupils

Many teachers are over 50. According to the Federal Statistical Office, in the 2024/25 school year exactly 35.4 per cent of teachers at general education schools were at least 50 years old. Some 25.4 per cent were between 50 and 59, and a further 10 per cent were 60 or older.

The German education system is therefore facing a major wave of retirements in the coming years. At the same time, it takes several years to train additional teachers.

Demand for teachers is likely to continue rising for the time being. According to the Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education, there were just under 11.2 million pupils in Germany in 2024. By 2032 the number is set to rise to almost 11.8 million, an increase of around 5.3 per cent. After that it is expected to fall slightly again because of smaller birth cohorts. By 2040, however, around 11.3 million pupils are still expected.

World.title: At least 132 killed and 570 injured in Colombia's biggest earthquake in years
World.content:
Colombian volunteers and rescuers sifted through rubble with bare hands and buckets on Tuesday, hunting for survivors following a massive 7.4-magnitude quake that has claimed the lives of at least 132 people and injured 570 others.

 

The quake struck several cities across Colombia's picturesque coffee region and Pacific shortly after 7:30 am on Monday, sending panicked residents onto the streets and damaging at least 1,500 buildings.

"People ran out naked, people jumped from the second floor of their homes" Wilmer Cuesta, a law student in Quibdo told the AFP news agency, recounting violent temors.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, just three days after being sworn into office, declared a state of emergency and vowed a concerted rescue effort.

In Cali, volunteers quickly went to work with picks, basic tools and their own hands to try to find survivors. Andres Felipe Mejia was among those who joined a makeshift crew.

"We are trying to get everyone out alive," he told AFP. "One of the rescuers asked anyone trapped to whistle and someone whistled back."

Rescue workers and residents search through the rubble after an earthquake struck Cali, 10 August, 2026 Santiago Saldarriaga / AP

"They pulled out a man and a baby, but the wife is still in there," he said near a pancaked multi-storey building.

Rescuers formed human chains to remove bricks and masonry, stopping every few minutes to listen for signs of life from those trapped below.

"A lot of people have come, with supplies, with food, helping the firefighters, helping the people," he said.

There were scenes of destruction in several cities, with furniture and fabrics sandwiched between concrete, walls and floors tossed into irregular angles and cabling strewn across roads.

The devastation comes less than two months after powerful twin quakes rattled neighbouring Venezuela, killing over 6,300 people and leaving tens of thousands homeless.

Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella leaves after leading an earthquake response meeting in Bogotá, 10 August, 2026 AP Photo

Hospitals in five Colombian cities were put on red alert on Monday and a nighttime curfew was declared in Cali, according to local authorities.

At least six local airports suspended operations, the civil aeronautics agency said.

Authorities warned the toll could rise as rescuers searched collapsed buildings across several cities.

In Manizales, an AFP journalist saw many damaged buildings, including the crumpled tower of the city's beloved neo-Gothic cathedral.

People prayed

Dentist Julian Pena was at home in Quibdo when he felt "very, very strong" shaking.

"People were praying in the street. It was overwhelming," he told AFP. "I ran outside carrying nothing and found hundreds of people there."

"There are many buildings with gaps, with cracks. There are others that have completely collapsed."

The quake was felt across Colombia, including the capital Bogotá, where crowds of people rushed out into the street in their pyjamas.

At a depth of 110 kilometres, the quake was also felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama.

Rescue workers and residents search through the rubble after an earthquake struck Cali, 10 August, 2026 AP Photo

Experts at the US Geological Survey said the quake was likely caused by movement along a deep fault within the Nazca tectonic plate.

All upcoming professional football matches have been postponed.

Messages of support came in from countries across the region and the world.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the United States was "closely monitoring" the situation and "stands ready to support the people of Colombia."

The US later announced $15.5 million (€13.4 million) in emergency relief.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU had mobilised Copernicus, the bloc’s satellite service, to help with rescue operations.

France, Mexico, Ecuador and Israel also offered assistance.

World.title: Explosive drone at Leipzig airport: Whose DNA was found on the device?
World.content:
On the night of 5 August 2026, Leipzig/Halle Airport came close to disaster when a drone fitted with explosives and a detonator appeared near a cargo aircraft operated by Ukrainian Antonov Airlines. Ammunition destined for Ukraine is reported to have been on board.

 

According to new findings, reported by the weekly Die Zeit, CCTV footage shows that at around 7.30 pm the drone deliberately flew towards the Ukrainian cargo aircraft and slammed into its wing. The device packed with Semtex did not explode on impact, however, but bounced off the Antonov and fell to the ground. The explosives appear to have become detached from the drone. According to Bild, the drone struck the Antonov close to the aircraft's fuel tank.

The drone was not picked up by any security system later that evening; instead, according to the report, an airport bus driver noticed the dangerous device four hours after the collision. He stepped on the drone with his foot. The explosives were apparently lying some distance away.

Police officers walking across a field on the grounds of Leipzig Airport, 7 August, 2026 AP Photo

DNA trace on the drone apparently leads to Lithuania

Five days after the incident at Leipzig Airport, Bild and Die Zeit report that investigators have secured DNA traces on the drone that failed to explode. No individual has yet been identified, but, according to Bild, there has been a match in the European DNA database and the trail apparently leads to Lithuania.

In addition, the DNA now secured is said to match that from an arson attack on 20 July 2024 on the DHL logistics centre at Leipzig Airport. The parcel bomb exploded on the ground rather than in the air on board the aircraft only because the DHL cargo plane was delayed.

Police vehicles are parked at Leipzig/Halle Airport, 6 August, 2026 AP Photo

Several suspects have been on trial in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius since the spring over the 2024 parcel bomb in Leipzig. The charge is "terrorism and sabotage on behalf of a foreign power". The Lithuanian prosecutor's office stated that the offences involving improvised explosive devices had been "organised and coordinated by citizens of the Russian Federation who are linked to the military intelligence services of the Russian Federation".

The defendants are alleged to have sent parcel bombs across Europe via freight services such as DHL and DDP. According to the Lithuanian authorities, the intended targets were Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. The EU judicial agency Eurojust in The Hague also believes Russia's military intelligence service, the GRU, was behind the 2024 wave of attacks.

Following the discovery of the drone in Leipzig, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office is investigating on suspicion of attempted detonation of an explosive device and of endangering air traffic. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has so far avoided any hint that Russia might be responsible for the drone incident. During a visit to Leipzig, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt spoke only of the possible involvement of "foreign powers".

The Kremlin denies any involvement by Russia in the drone attack on Leipzig. On Telegram, the Russian embassy in Berlin described it as a "provocation directed against Moscow" and warned of "a new wave of anti-Russian hysteria in Germany".

World.title: Vietnam's VinSpace taps SpaceX for first satellite launches
World.content:
Vietnam's first private space company is turning to Elon Musk's SpaceX to get its first satellites into orbit. The deal comes as Vietnam steps up efforts to build its own space industry and become a regional space power.

Vietnam's only private space company on Tuesday signed a deal with SpaceX to launch its first satellites into orbit next year.

The satellites will fly aboard a 2027 mission under SpaceX's Transporter rideshare program, which allows multiple customers to share the same rocket and split satellite launch costs.

What do we know about VinSpace and SpaceX?

The company, VinSpace, said it would develop and operate the satellites itself, using the missions to test technology in orbit and pave the way for future commercial services.

"Reliable access to space is fundamental to turning satellite innovation into operational missions," VinSpace CEO Thu Vu said.

The company did not disclose how many satellites it plans to launch, their specifications or the value of the contract with Elon Musk's SpaceX.

What is VinSpace?

VinSpace was established in November 2025 by Vingroup, Vietnam's largest privately-owned conglomerate.

The group was founded by Pham Nhat Vuong, Vietnam's richest man. It has interests ranging from real estate, retail and tourism to healthcare and education.

China's new rocket heats up space race, challenging SpaceX To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In recent years, Vingroup has increasingly expanded into technology, including electric vehicles, artificial intelligence, robotics and aerospace.

VinSpace says it ultimately wants to become a full-service aerospace company, with capabilities spanning satellite design and manufacturing, launch management, satellite operations and space-based data services.

What are Vietnam's ambitions in space?

Vietnam has been building its space capabilities for decades but remains a relatively small player in the global industry.

It launched its first telecommunications satellite in 2008 and a second in 2012.

The government has set a goal of becoming a mid-level space power in Southeast Asia by 2030, with satellite technology seen as part of a wider drive to develop high-tech industries.

In March, Vietnam opened a major space science and technology center at Hanoi's Hoa Lac High-Tech Park, aimed at expanding domestic satellite development and the use of space-based data.

In April, Vietnam licensed SpaceX's Starlink for its first large-scale trial of satellite internet, which uses thousands of low-Earth-orbit satellites to provide high-speed connectivity.

Edited by: Rob Turner

World.title: Syria sentences Bashar Assad to death in absentia
World.content:
A Syrian court has sentenced ousted President Bashar Assad to death in absentia. The ruling comes more than a year and a half after the former dictator was overthrown and fled to Russia.

A Syrian court on Tuesday sentenced former President Bashar Assad to death in absentia.

Assad was ousted in December 2024 after rebel forces swept into Damascus, ending more than five decades of rule by the Assad family.

He fled to Russia, where he was granted asylum, while Syria's new authorities have begun pursuing former officials over alleged crimes committed during the country's civil war.

The court also handed the death penalty to Atef Najib, a senior security official under Assad's rule and a cousin of the former dictator. He was arrested while trying to flee the country in January 2025.

World.title: How one German city is preparing for climate extremes
World.content:
Western Europe has recorded its hottest-ever June and July, and extreme weather from wildfires to storms is here to stay. How can we adapt to what seems to be the new normal? Cities like Kiel are trying new ideas.

In October 2023, the worst storm surge in more than 150 years hit the Baltic Sea coast . It destroyed dikes, collapsed coastal cliffs and devastated marinas in the northern German state of Schleswig-Holstein and parts of southern Denmark.

The catastrophic surge wiped away 2.68 meters (8.79 feet) of coastal bluff in Kiel, a port city and Schleswig-Holstein's capital. That was more than four times the yearly average lost over the previous two decades.

Human-caused climate change is supercharging extreme weather such as storms. And in coastal cities like Kiel, the consequences are already impossible to ignore.

"The impacts of climate change are hardly abstract in Kiel," said Martina Baum, who heads the city's climate adaptation division. "Since at least the 2023 storm surge, we have all been reminded of the profound effects it can have on us, on our daily lives, and on the environment around us."

Those effects are forcing Kiel — among the first cities to declare a climate emergency back in 2019 — to rethink its design, and how it works. It has since become a front-runner in adapting to the realities of a changing climate, establishing Baum's division in 2025 to help make the city more resilient to weather extremes and adopting an adaptation plan in February 2026 to step up those measures.

Is climate adaptation giving up on fighting climate change?

For city officials like Baum, adaptation is not a substitute for cutting the fossil fuel emissions heating the planet. Climate protection remains the first line of defense, because limiting warming will reduce future damage.

"For a long time, there was hesitation to engage officially with the issue of climate change adaptation. I also felt uneasy about it at first, because it felt as though it would somehow take the pressure off climate protection efforts," Baum told DW.

But the move to adaptation in Kiel reflects what's happening in other cities around the world from Santa Cruz in the US to Quezon City in the Philippines , as governments increasingly prepare for the impacts of heat, heavier rainfall and stronger storm surges that are already here.

With days getting hotter, Quezon City in the Philippines has also intensified its adaptation plans Image: Aaron Favila/AP Photo/picture alliance

That doesn't mean climate protection and adaptation always align. Installing power-hungry air-conditioning in housing, daycare or senior centers, for instance, protects vulnerable people in heat waves. But it increases energy consumption, "which would run counter to climate protection goals," Baum said.

"Even if we use renewable energy, demand is not yet covered by renewable sources 100% of the time, so any additional energy we consume will ultimately result in the emission of climate-damaging greenhouse gases," she added.

Redesigning cities for unavoidable impacts

While AC will sometimes be necessary, Kiel is working on solutions that cool the city naturally. It's adding vegetation to building facades, redesigning a park to channel cooler air into the city center, and making it easier for residents to access permits, information and grants for adaptation projects.

The city is also testing which tree species can survive future conditions. A decade ago, Kiel planted five specimens each of 20 different species to find out which can best withstand heat, drought and salt spray from the nearby Baltic Sea.

Kolkata's tree ambulance rushes to save urban trees To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trees provide shade, cool streets by roughly 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) and improve air quality, but not every species will thrive as the climate changes.

"There is no one-size-fits-all climate tree; different sites require different tree species," said Nicole Holz, who works in the department responsible for the city's green spaces.

The research requires patience.

"It's going to take some 20, 30 years until you get some real results," said Petra Holtappel, head of the same department.

Living differently: No more daytime soccer?

Adapting to climate change will also require changes to daily life, said Baum. Children, for example, may no longer be able to play soccer tournaments at 3 p.m. because it's too hot.

It may become the new normal to play only during certain times of the day Image: Fabio Teixeira/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Although Kiel is getting warmer, it is expected to fare better than much hotter cities in Southern or Central Europe when it comes to heat. Still, the city is vulnerable to more storm surges and heavy rain and needs more retention areas to manage all that excess water. The city is dredging the park's pond to store stormwater during heavy rainfall, but is also exploring other ideas.

"One idea is what's known as multi-use design, meaning that in future, a soccer pitch could be built slightly lower than the surrounding area. During periods of heavy rain, water could then be directed there and allowed to gradually infiltrate into the ground or evaporate," Baum said.

The downside is the pitch might be unusable for up to 60 days a year, she added. But residents would need accept that, said Baum, who emphasized the need for greater public debate about adaptation measures.

How to reach people who don't think about the climate?

Helping residents understand those trade-offs and what's at stake is part of Annafried Stürmer's work. Stürmer organizes educational events, leads public excursions with scientists and attends neighborhood fairs to meet people who might not otherwise engage with climate issues.

At Kiel Week in June, the world's biggest annual sailing event, Stürmer displayed a map showing city flood risk from extreme rainfall.

The 2023 storm surge caused caused millions of euro in damage in the port city of Kiel Image: Daniel Bockwoldt/dpa/picture alliance

"People often find that interesting, because it doesn't immediately seem like it's connected to climate change. Instead, the initial reaction is , 'Wow, if we get one of those intense heavy rainfall events, my house could be in serious trouble,' or 'My backyard could end up flooded,'" Stürmer said.

Stürmer has often found it easier to talk about climate adaptation than about climate change, because the former is more tangible.

"It's easier to talk about the need for a better-developed sewer system to handle heavy rainfall, or about planting different types of trees and vegetation, than it is to talk about reducing CO2 emissions," Stürmer told DW.

Recent record heat waves have made the adaptation conservation more urgent too.

"People noticed that it hadn't been as hot before," she said, adding residents increasingly recognize the need to protect children, the elderly, pregnant women and outdoor workers.

Climate adaptation not 'optional'

Even with growing public awareness of the need for adaptation, funding remains a problem in cash-strapped Kiel. Still seen as optional, climate action can quickly come under pressure when budgets tighten.

"I disagree with the idea that climate adaptation and climate action are optional responsibilities. I keep asking myself: what are the alternatives?" Baum said. "After all, it has been demonstrated time and again that investing in climate adaptation and climate mitigation will simply pay off."

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

08/11/2026 August 11, 2026 Tamil Nadu calls to scrap nationwide medical college entrance examination

The Tamil Nadu government proposed admissions for medical colleges based on students' grades in Class 12 [FILE: September 13, 2020] Image: Arun Sankar/AFP/Getty Images

Tamil Nadu's state legislature on Tuesday passed a resolution urging the central government to scrap the nationwide medical college entrance examination, media reports said.

Health Minister KG Arunraj said the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (NEET) exam undermined social justice and disadvantaged rural and poorer students by increasing reliance on costly coaching centers, according to the reports.

The Tamil Nadu government instead proposed admissions for medical colleges based on students' grades in Class 12.

The motion was supported by all parties, with the lone lawmaker from Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) walking out during the proceedings, reports said.

The NEET exam has been in the news in India since the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) launched a protest following the cancellation of the test in May, after authorities found its question paper was leaked.

The cancellation of the highly competitive NEET exam sparked outrage across the country.

The CJP protests, which started in New Delhi and then spread across the country, forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan last month.

World.title: Germany news: Rhine levels could cause production cuts
World.content:
Skip next section What you need to know about low river water levels

08/11/2026 August 11, 2026 What you need to know about low river water levels

The level of 19 cm reached last week in Kaub was already a record — but worse is to come Image: 5VISION.NEWS/IMAGO

Water levels in several rivers in Germany, including the Rhine, have hit record lows that are well below normal for this time of year, causing severe disruptions to river traffic, with ships cutting their loads by around 80%.

The water shortage comes amid a prolonged dry period in Germany, accompanied by frequent heat waves, both of which are attributed by scientists partly to the effects of human-induced climate change.

But why is the situation so serious for Germany, and what are the key terms in connection with low water levels?

The Rhine: A vital transport waterway

The Rhine has been used as a transport corridor for much of western Europe since Roman times.

It is the most important waterway in Europe, connecting industrial regions in Germany, Switzerland and other countries with big North Sea ports, including Rotterdam in the Netherlands.

Although only one in 10 tons of freight in Germany is transported via rivers such as the Rhine, they are much used for certain goods, including ore, oil, chemical products and coal.

As a result, industries that depend on these for their production are likely to be forced to cut their output, as not only is supply reduced in the current situation, but transport prices have also gone up massively.

What are river gauge measurements?

The depth of water in German rivers is measured by gauges (Pegel) situated at strategic points on their course.

These gauges, which are mostly located near the banks of a river, measure the depth of the river over an arbitrarily selected baseline.

This means the measurements are only an indication of the actual navigable depth, which can be much more.

For instance, although the gauge at the town of Kaub currently measures 16 cm (6.3 inches), the depth of the river in the channel used by shipping there is around 129 cm.

Why is the gauge at Kaub so important?

Kaub is situated on the Middle Rhine between St. Goar and Budenheim.

This section of river is seen as a chokepoint for shipping on the Rhine, as the navigable channel is not as well developed as in other places.

It has also long been used since 1856 as a key location to measure low water levels in the Rhine.

The previous lowest measurement in Kaub was 25 cm (9.8 inches) on October 22, 2018.

The present measurement of 16 cm is thus already a historic low — and it is expected to sink to single figures in the next few days.

President Donald Trump said that the US has cleared the Strait of Hormuz of mines, and that the critical trade route was open to commercial traffic.

Trump told reporters at the White House that the US had 100% control of the waterway.

"A little bit complex because they [Iran] will, on occasion, drop a mine, and we find the mines. You know, we've mine swept the entire Strait," he said.

Trump's comments came as Washington and Tehran have been negotiating the full reopening of the strait for some time. Iran has linked the route's reopening to concessions from the US and its allies while affirming plans to charge commercial vessels passing through the strait.

Over the last weekend, US Vice President JD Vance said that Iran had laid a large number of mines in the Strait at he beginning of the war.

World.title: Trump pushes overhaul of US policy on vaccines for children
World.content:
In an executive order, President Trump calls for fewer recommended childhood vaccinations and more spacing between shots. Medical experts say the changes lack scientific backing and could leave children less protected.

On Monday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order seeking sweeping changes to the US's childhood vaccine policy, including fewer recommended immunizations and more separate appointments for children to receive them.

The order calls for the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, known as MMR, to be separated into three single-disease shots. It also advocates administering childhood immunizations at separate medical visits whenever possible.

A healthcare worker prepares an MMR vaccination at a health center in Texas [FILE: April 8, 2025] Image: Annie Rice/AP Photo/picture alliance

Trump described the move as a "major victory for parents rights, religious and constitutional rights, and for the gold standard science."

What changes does Trump want for childhood vaccines?

The order says the federal government will support 11 core childhood vaccinations and advises states and territories to review vaccine requirements for school enrollment.

However, Washington cannot directly determine most school vaccine mandates, which are largely set by individual states. On those requirements, Trump's order is therefore primarily a recommendation.

The order also directs the Health and Human Services Department to improve vaccine research and develop a plan to make separate measles, mumps and rubella vaccines available in the US. Such single-antigen vaccines are not currently licensed there.

US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has long questioned established vaccine recommendations and promoted a disproven link between vaccines and autism Image: Andrew Leyden/ZUMA/picture alliance

Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. had already sought in January to remove vaccines against six of 17 diseases from the childhood schedule. A federal judge later blocked those changes while legal proceedings continue. Monday's order reaffirms much of that overhaul.

Why do experts oppose spacing out vaccines?

Public health experts say childhood vaccination schedules are based on extensive research into when and how vaccines can safely be administered together. Safety monitoring continues after vaccines are introduced.

They warn that spreading shots across more appointments can leave children vulnerable to preventable diseases for longer and increase the risk that later doses are delayed or missed.

Vaccine maker Merck said there was no published scientific evidence showing any benefit from splitting the MMR vaccine. Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, estimated that developing and approving separate vaccines in the US could take more than a decade.

"We're advising that you continue to give children a vaccine that has decades of safety data," said Aaron M. Milstone, a member of the AAP Committee on Infectious Diseases.

What does Trump say about vaccines and autism?

Speaking in the Oval Office, Trump repeatedly suggested that the number or timing of childhood vaccines could be linked to rising rates of autism spectrum disorder.

Scientific consensus and decades of studies have found no link between vaccination and autism.

Kennedy has also repeatedly promoted the disproven connection. He founded an anti-vaccine nonprofit before joining the administration.

How have experts reacted to Trump's vaccine order?

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, a physician and chairman of the Senate health committee, condemned the move.

"I'm a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The president does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy said, adding that splitting combination vaccines "will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots."

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy, a physician, has sharply criticized Trump's executive order on childhood vaccines, saying it could leave children less protected [FILE: May 19, 2026] Image: Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Cassidy cast the decisive vote to confirm Kennedy as health secretary in 2025 despite concerns over his vaccine skepticism. He lost his Republican primary in May to a Trump-backed challenger and is due to leave office in January.

New York City Health Commissioner Alister Martin said the order was based "in politics and conspiracy theories."

"Fortunately, vaccination recommendations are not set by the president, nor should they be," Martin said.

Why is the timing of Trump's vaccine push significant?

The policy shift comes as the United States experiences its worst measles outbreak in 35 years and children prepare to return to school.

Critics have accused Kennedy of contributing to vaccine hesitancy through years of questioning established immunizations.

The renewed focus on vaccines also marks a shift from the administration's recent emphasis on less divisive health policies, including healthy eating, drug price negotiations and efforts to combat medical fraud ahead of November's midterm elections.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Turkey MPs back historic law on reintegrating PKK militants
World.content:
Turkey's parliament has taken a major step toward ending four decades of conflict with the PKK. The new law sets out how some militants can return to civilian life, but leaves Abdullah Ocalan's future unresolved.

Turkey's parliament on Monday approved legislation offering a conditional pardon and legal protections to thousands of members of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK).

After around 12 hours of debate, lawmakers voted 468 to 88 in favor of the 12-article bill, with six abstentions. It was backed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's AK Party, its nationalist MHP allies and the pro-Kurdish DEM party.

What does Turkey's new PKK law provide?

The law sets out procedures for the PKK's disarmament and dissolution and the reintegration of some members into civilian life. The government has stressed that it is not a general amnesty.

Some prison sentences would be suspended, while investigations and trials could be postponed for five or 10 years depending on the offense.

If those covered commit no terrorism-related crime during that period, cases would be dropped and sentences considered served.

Turkish lawmakers debated the bill for around 12 hours before voting on the legislation Image: Mustafa Kaya/Xinhua/picture alliance

Around 3,500 PKK-linked detainees could initially be released, lawmakers said. Media reports suggest exiled members and fighters in Iraq and Syria could also benefit.

People convicted of intentional killings and some serving life sentences are excluded.

When will the law take effect?

The measures will only come into force once Turkey's National Security Council confirms that the PKK has dissolved and surrendered all weapons.

Those seeking to benefit would then have six months to apply. Ministerial and parliamentary committees are also due to monitor the process.

Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz hailed the vote as a 'historic step' toward ending the decades-long conflict with the PKK [FILE: March 27, 2026] Image: Ahmet Okur/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO

Turkey’s Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz called the vote a "historic step", saying "the 468 'yes' votes are of the utmost importance in terms of political consensus".

What happens to Abdullah Ocalan?

The law does not cover imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan, 77, who has been held on Imrali island near Istanbul since 1999.

Yilmaz said Ocalan's case "does not fall within the scope of this law", but added that he could remain "in a position to contribute to the peace process".

Ocalan has been central to the initiative. In February 2025, he urged the PKK to disarm and dissolve and pursue Kurdish rights through democratic means.

This latest image of imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan was provided by the pro-Kurdish DEM party [FILE: February 27, 2026] Image: DEM

The PKK announced its dissolution in May 2025. Two months later, militants symbolically burned weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq and the group said it was withdrawing fighters from Turkey.

What does the PKK say?

The PKK has called the legislation a "beginning" but said it contains "serious shortcomings and deficiencies."

It has demanded Ocalan's release and said the process can move forward only if he "lives and works freely."

The group also said fighters would not return without guarantees that they could engage in politics without prosecution over their views or organizations.

Pro-Kurdish DEM lawmaker Gulistan Kilic Kocyigit said: "The people of Turkey, who have paid a heavy price for many years, now have an opportunity to consolidate peace and build democracy."

Why is the bill controversial?

Nationalist opposition lawmakers accuse the government of making concessions to the PKK.

"How can you negotiate with terrorists? You said they would be laying down their weapons unconditionally," said Turhan Comez, a lawmaker with the nationalist opposition Iyi party.

Turkey: An end to the Kurdish conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Iyi Party leader Musavat Dervisoglu also said the law "would pave the way" for Erdogan to remain in power. Erdogan could run again if parliament calls an early election during his current term.

Why does the conflict matter?

The PKK launched its insurgency in 1984. More than 40,000 people have been killed, and the conflict has caused major economic damage in Kurdish-majority southeastern Turkey and fueled decades of political and social division.

The PKK initially sought an independent Kurdish state but later shifted toward demands for autonomy and expanded rights.

It is designated a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States and the European Union.

Previous peace efforts failed, most recently in 2015.

The initiative could also have regional effects, including closer Turkish-Iraqi ties and implications for efforts to integrate areas in Syria administered by the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) with Damascus.

The SDF's dominant militia, the People's Defense Units (YPG), is seen as an offshoot of the PKK, and is considered by Ankara to be a terrorist organization.
