World.title: The Nation Is Now: Let the Youth Share Its Present
World.content:
Every 12th of August, organizations parade brilliant young minds across articles for International Youth Day. The youth are handed microphones, seated on panels, and branded with big bold letters: Aspiring student-leaders, the upcoming generation, the future.

They invite us, the youth, into a room, almost as mascots, because once we voice modern ideas that go against the set-in-stone standard, the script flips. Despite all those inspirational youth stories, there is a reality we, the youth, face every day—one where we are constantly told to tone it down and rewrite our scripts.

Truth is, when we speak about certain topics—such as the psychological toll of navigating such an uncertain future, or challenging deeply ingrained habits that society has accepted as the norm—we are mostly dismissed and not taken seriously.

This has created a sort of branding for today’s youth: Too sensitive, too woke. Talk about climate change and geopolitical tensions, and we are told that we are worrying about things that don’t even touch us. They frame it as mere unearned anxiety.

There would be mocking dismissals on social media; one that caught my eye the most was: “Ganitong kahina na ba ang pag-asa ng bayan na sinasabi ni Rizal?”

How certain corners of society love to throw Jose Rizal’s words in our faces when we fall short of their expectations and outdated standards of the past, which they call “tough love”. Words that are meant to fuel the youth are twisted into weaponized shame for showing vulnerability. At the same time, it is also used to burden us with being the hope of this world, while simultaneously denying agency to act like it.

The youth is seen as incapable, with this generation’s more inclusive empathy synonymous with weakness—as if speaking up in dysfunctional systems that single us out doesn’t already take a lot of courage.

“Masyado ka pang bata para makaintindi.”

It is something we relentlessly hear when we share our perspective on an issue, as if our youth takes away our participation chances. We are told to wait our turn, and wait until we’re older to be taken seriously.

Ang kabataan ang pag-asa ng bayan.

This is often viewed as the youth being the hope promised for our nation. However, hope is a destination we will never reach if we are not allowed to move today. The nation is not a future state. It doesn’t wait for us in twenty years while we are required to go through tests of suffering to earn respect; it is a present reality that does not pause for us to grow up.

We are living through today’s crises now, and we will live through them in decades down the line. Eventually, there will be a new generation born into whatever chaos exists by then, and offer us a new perspective in return. We should perpetuate a cycle which acknowledges that experience isn’t just how many decades a person has lived; it is proximity to a problem.

And the youth’s proximity to these global problems is undeniable—because our lived reality now is telling us what kind of fallout we are surviving today, and what kind of world we are going to inherit tomorrow.

A cycle of patterns and decisions being made for us but not truly seeing us.

People always say they stand for the youth, but it’s about time we stand with the youth.

We are not passive watchers, beneficiaries, or charity cases to be given a seat and a microphone for the sake of attention and buzzwords. We are also living through one world crisis after another, and we are not sitting and waiting for decades to earn the right to worry and act.

This doesn’t mean that hard-earned wisdom of the older generations goes unnoticed, but we must bridge the gap between those who lived the past and the ticking realities of the present. The past offers guidance, but it does not give us the momentum to address today’s issues because that is something within us, those who are born and grew up in this new era.

But with this momentum we are not asking to be put on a pedestal of some sort. Respect comes with responsibility, and failure to meet those responsibilities comes with consequences. There will be accountability, but let accountability mean owning our mistakes and working to be better, and not shut out the entirety of the youth’s validity.

And standing with the youth starts right there and not with grand institutional gestures, but with something smaller in size but meaningful: being comfortable with listening and adapting, being open to modern realities such as unlearning the habits of silent endurance, weighing our insights on national news as valid concerns.

To stand with the youth means viewing our enthusiasm as necessary urgency and not just pure youthful idealism. It means letting us be capable thinkers of today, instead of distant leaders of a tomorrow that may never come—and this starts with truly understanding what is being asked of us in the first place.

Ang kabataan ang pag-asa ng Bayan.

Rizal wrote that immortalized masterpiece at just eighteen years old, with nothing but a pen he exposed the cruelty of the Spanish colonial rule, and united Filipinos—all of which happened during most of his youth.

Rizal did not wait for a future to act. He did not wait for his turn, because if he did, there would be no rightful future to act in.

Rizal was acting in the heat of his present moment, our historical past. If we don’t act now, what kind of historical past are we writing for the future? What visions will the future see when they lay their eyes on us?

Are we the youth who stood for something, or the youth who stood for nothing?

We are not going to wait to become citizens of this country because the nation is now and forever will be in motion. The world doesn’t stop spinning—the past, the present, and our future are a history that never stops watching us—and we are already both participants and collateral of this very world.

To stand with the youth is to recognize that the nation is breathing and surviving right now, and we are no longer waiting for tomorrow.

We are already here.

World.title: Grave threats case filed vs Sara Duterte over assassination remarks
World.content:
MEET. Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Senate on July 7, 2026, to meet with her lawyers but did attend her impeachment trial.

(1st UPDATE) 'Given these serious legal issues, the Vice President will exercise all available legal remedies in due course,' Duterte's lawyer Paul Lawrence Lim says

MANILA, Philippines – Department of Justice (DOJ) prosecutors filed three counts of grave threats case against Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday, August 11, in relation to statements she made against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family in 2024.

“We confirm that the [case] for grave threats against Vice President Sara Duterte was filed today, August 11, 2026, at around 1:30 pm with the Office of the Clerk of Court of the Quezon City Regional Trial Court,” DOJ spokesperson Raphael Martinez told reporters.

This is the same grave threats allegation in Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial which was investigated by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI).

The filing of the case against Duterte means that DOJ prosecutors found prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction or enough evidence to ensure that the case would lead to a guilty verdict.

“The inciting to sedition case was dismissed,” Martinez added.

Duterte’s legal team, in a statement on Tuesday afternoon, confirmed the filing of cases against the Vice President, adding that they had anticipated and prepared for this outcome.

“Under our laws, the Vice President continues to be presumed innocent and is confident that the charges against her will ultimately be dismissed. Equally important, as a sitting impeachable officer, the Vice President may not be prosecuted for an alleged offense that is also the subject of an impeachment case,” said Duterte’s lawyer Paul Lawrence Lim.

“Given these serious legal issues, the Vice President will exercise all available legal remedies in due course,” he added.

In November 2025, the NBI filed criminal complaints of grave threats and inciting to sedition against the Vice President over her statement that she had allegedly arranged to assassinate Marcos, First lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former speaker Martin Romualdez if she were killed first.

These allegations stemmed from the Vice President’s midnight virtual press conference on November 23, 2024, where she told her supporters not to worry about her safety as she had already “talked to someone” to ensure that if she gets killed, that person should assassinate Marcos and his family members. Duterte reiterated at the time that she was not joking.

Of the four articles of impeachment or cases against Duterte at the Senate impeachment court, the prosecution first presented its evidence for grave threats or the fourth article. House prosecutors presented three witnesses from the NBI, including incumbent Director Melvin Matibag.

No effects on impeachment

Unlike the president, the vice president does not enjoy legal immunity.



Several legal experts, including one of the framers of the 1987 Constitution, Father Joaquin Bernas, had said that the country’s second in command is not immune from suit. (READ: ‘Vice President does not enjoy immunity’)

The President, on the other hand, enjoys immunity while in office, based on tradition and jurisprudence. This is to ensure that the President can “fully attend to his duties and functions.”

Meanwhile, University of the Philippines College of Law professor and constitutional law expert Dan Gatmaytan explained to Rappler that the grave threats case won’t affect the Senate trial. This is despite them having the same set of allegations.

“The cases can proceed simultaneously. There is no rule that says the impeachment process must be terminated before the criminal case can proceed,” Gatmaytan told Rappler.

“To be guilty in the criminal case, the prosecution must show guilt beyond reasonable doubt. This is not the same standard or quantum of evidence that is required in the impeachment case because it is not a criminal case,” he added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Ateneo, ex-coach Tab Baldwin fined P4.9 million over work permit violations
World.content:
EMBATTLED. Former Ateneo men’s basketball coach Tab Baldwin attends the Department of Labor and Employment's clarificatory hearing on the validity of his Alien Employment Permit on June 29, 2026. The hearing, led by Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino, is part of the department’s review of Baldwin’s employment documents.

DOLE's decision to fine Ateneo and Tab Baldwin comes shortly after the university insisted that the former men's basketball coach was a consultant, not an employee

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE) slapped the Ateneo de Manila University and its former men’s basketball coach Thomas Anthony “Tab” Baldwin with a P4.9 million administrative fine on Tuesday, August 11.

Baldwin was found to have been working for the university from December 1, 2015 to September 28, 2016 without a valid Alien Employment Permit (AEP).

An AEP, issued by DOLE, allows foreign nationals to legally work in the Philippines so long as it is proven that there are no Filipino citizens able or willing to perform the same services.

The ex-coach — a dual citizen of the US and New Zealand — was then ordered to pay a P10,000 fine to cover the one-year period that he worked without a valid AEP. Ateneo was asked to pay the same fine of P10,000 for having Baldwin render his services without the AEP.

The DOLE also held Baldwin liable for failing to secure a Certificate of Exemption, which is given to foreign nationals to signify that they can work in the Philippines without having to obtain an AEP. Baldwin’s continued work without this legal document counts as noncompliance.

Each day of violation constitutes a fine of P10,000. This means that Baldwin would have to pay an administrative fine of P4.9 million to account for each of the 490 days he worked in the Philippines without the necessary permits from February 10, 2025, until his eventual resignation on June 15, 2026.

According to DOLE, the Ateneo administration was held “jointly and solidarily liable” with the 68-year-old basketball coach to settle the P4.9 million fine. The counsels of both parties will explore any legal remedies under applicable laws.

Baldwin and Ateneo have been the subject of public scrutiny since June after a tragic team building incident in Dipaculao, Aurora led to the deaths of players Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili.

DOLE’s move to fine Ateneo and Baldwin comes just a month after the university told the government agency that Baldwin was not an employee, but a consultant.

Lawyer Jose Feliciano — who helped Baldwin obtain his quota immigrant visa and an alien certificate of registration (ACR) from the Bureau of Immigration — said he did not see the need for Baldwin to apply for an AEP as he is already a resident alien.

Feliciano argued that under Article 40 of the Labor Code, resident aliens are exempted from acquiring AEPs.

Still, Baldwin failed to obtain his Certificate of Exemption before continuing his work as a basketball coach in the Philippines.

As of 2025, foreign individuals who can apply for the Certificate of Exemption must fall into these categories:

Refugees and stateless persons recognized by the Department of Justice

Those who come to the Philippines to teach, present, or conduct research studies in universities and colleges as visiting, exchange, or adjunct professors under formal agreements between the universities and colleges in the Philippines and the foreign ones, or between the Philippine government and foreign government

Permanent resident foreign nationals and probationary or temporary resident visa holders

Officers or any employees working in the Embassy by reason of extra-territoriality principle

Accredited officials and personnel (and their dependent spouses) from international organizations that the Philippine government has an established agreement with

Officers or staff of peacekeeping or international organizations deployed in the Philippines or by NGOs that have been accredited or endorsed by related government agencies

Beyond issues related to Baldwin’s employment and his handling of the men’s basketball team, his estranged wife Efi also accused Ateneo of ignoring her repeated pleas to keep the coach away from children as they are “not safe around him.”

The UAAP has since “perpetually banned” Baldwin and has moved to allow the Ateneo Blue Eagles to compete in season 89 of the premier collegiate sports league. – Rappler.com

World.title: What removal of mandatory ‘spiral progression’ means for K to 12 program
World.content:
OPENING. Students of Navarro Elementary School in General Trias City, Cavite, attend the first day of classes for school year 2026-2027 on June 8, 2026.

A new amendment to the Enhanced Basic Education Act essentially grants the Department of Education freedom from a ‘one-size-fits-all’ approach to teaching

MANILA, Philippines – After over a decade of implementation, Republic Act No. 10533 or the Enhanced Basic Education Act of 2013, which institutionalized the K to 12 program, was amended in a bid to improve the quality of learning in the country.

Republic Act (RA) No. 12322 removed the mandatory use of a “spiral progression” approach in implementing the curriculum. It lapsed into law on August 2, and was publicized on the Official Gazette website on August 5.

Section 5 of the K to 12 law now provides: “The curriculum shall employ the approach deemed most effective by the DepEd (Department of Education) to ensure mastery of knowledge and skills after each level.”

It also said that the curriculum and approach will be subjected to review at least once every five years.

The amendment came nearly two years since the discontinuation of the use of mother tongue as the language of instruction from kindergarten to Grade 3, a specific provision of the K to 12 law. The discontinuation was through RA 12027, which lapsed into law in October 2024.

What is spiral progression?

Spiral progression is a curriculum approach where the concepts taught are revisited with increasing depth and complexity as students progress through their schooling.

Let’s take for example how science is taught in basic education.

Before the K to 12 program, each level in high school focused only on a single discipline (general science for freshmen, biology for sophomores, chemistry for juniors, and physics for seniors). This is called a discipline-based approach.

But under the K to 12 program’s spiral progression, Grade 7 to 10 learners or junior high school students study all of these disciplines in one academic year, with the lessons becoming more complex at each grade level.

During a Senate basic education committee hearing in January, Education Undersecretary Carmela Oracion said spiral progression is a “sound, research-based curriculum principle.”

Screenshot from the Senate’s YouTube video

She said one of the advantages of the approach is cumulative mastery, as concepts return every school year with added depth.

Other advantages include stronger retention of lessons, smooth connection of topics across grade levels, and the prevention of learning gaps as missed skills can be learned in later levels.

But Oracion, who was also a math teacher, acknowledged that spiral progression may not be suitable for some subjects. During the Senate committee hearing, she specifically said a discipline-based curriculum may be more suitable for mathematics and science in high school.

The DepEd official explained that a discipline-based approach may provide a deeper subject focus as well as clearer pacing and coverage with its straightforward scope per grade level. It could also build specialization for learners as they stay longer on a topic before moving on to the next.

The Philippine experience

In 2023, the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) flagged that teachers were challenged by spiral progression and were concerned about repetitive lessons throughout the curriculum.

In its research, EDCOM 2 found studies as early as 2014 saying that teachers criticized the lack of depth and concentration for each science discipline under the K to 12 program’s spiral progression approach.

According to the commission, the approach “conflicts with the preservice training of teachers, in which they specialize in one discipline only.”

There is also another finding that six out of 10 high school teachers handle subjects they “did not major in college”.

“We see that when the spiral progression is well-designed, focused, and supported by teacher capacity — which we may not have yet at a very good state in the country — this can contribute to strong learner outcomes and international performance,” Oracion told the Senate basic education committee in January.

“And maybe that’s the reason why the spiral progression approach even in secondary school mathematics and science is working very well in Singapore and Japan,” she said.

Singapore consistently tops the Programme for International Student Assessment or PISA rankings, while the Philippines is still among the countries with poor proficiency in reading, mathematics, and science for young learners.

Screenshot from the Senate’s YouTube video

Welcoming flexibility

The amendment has granted the DepEd freedom from a “one-size-fits-all” approach, bringing back flexibility in determining the teaching methods suited for every class.

The DepEd said it allows science and mathematics teachers to “adopt mastery-based learning or alternative methods, ensuring learners thoroughly understand foundational concepts before advancing.”

The development does not mean teachers are barred from using spiral progression. It does not mean that schools will see immediate curriculum changes either, as implementing rules and regulations still have to be crafted.

The DepEd clarified that any adjustments to instructional delivery “remain subject to thorough review, pedagogical evidence, and practical considerations, including textbook supply and teacher training.”

“This update is about maintaining the flexibility our curriculum experts and field officers need to address learning gaps,” Education Secretary Sonny Angara said. “Our focus remains on stability in our schools and ensuring our teaching strategies directly improve learner outcomes.”

The DepEd said all other curriculum standards under the law “remain intact.”

In 2024, the agency began the phased rollout of the Matatag curriculum, or the revised K to 10 curriculum, lessening the number of learning areas for students to focus on foundational skills.

In 2025, the agency started the Strengthened Senior High School Program to reduce learning tracks and extend work immersion hours, in a bid to address job mismatch after graduation from SHS.

The curriculum approach is just one of the many issues in the country’s education sector, which continues to face budget constraints, school congestion, classroom shortages, insufficient textbooks and other resources, and heavy workload for teachers, among others. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
World.content:

World.title: Top 10 agencies with biggest allocations in proposed 2027 budget
World.content:
2027 BUDGET. Department of Budget and Management Acting Secretary Kim De Leon (right) turnsover the proposed P7.2-trillion National Expenditure Program for 2027 to House Speaker Bojie Dy III (left) on August 11, 2026.

Committee on Appropriations chairperson Mika Suansing says the budget deliberations will begin on Monday, August 17

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) on Tuesday, August 11, formally submitted the proposed P7.2-trillion National Expenditure Program (NEP) for 2027 to the House of Representatives and the Senate.

The Department of Education (DepEd) has the biggest proposed allocation at P976 billion or 13.55% of the total expenditure program, in line with the constitutional mandate to prioritize education in the national budget.

It is followed by the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), which has a proposed allocation of P664 billion. Of this amount, P107.4 billion, or about 16% of the agency’s total proposed budget, is earmarked for flood control projects.

Here are the 10 agencies and sectors with the biggest proposed allocations under the 2027 NEP, according to DBM Acting Secretary Kim de Leon:

According to De Leon, the government also allocated P10.773 billion for confidential and intelligence funds in the 2027 budget proposal. Of this amount, P4.368 billion is for confidential funds, while P6.405 billion is for intelligence funds.

“We wish to reiterate that the use of confidential and intelligence funds remains subject to existing budgeting, utilization, liquidation, and auditing rules to ensure accountability and that the funds are used solely for their intended purposes,” De Leon said.

Confidential funds have come under scrutiny in recent years after the Commission on Audit flagged the funds’ use by Vice President Sara Duterte’s Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education when she headed it.

The alleged misuse of confidential funds is among the grounds cited in the impeachment case against Duterte.

The turnover of the NEP to the House of Representatives marks the beginning of the budget cycle in the legislative branch. Committee on Appropriations chairperson and Nueva Ecija 1st District Representative Mika Suansing said that the budget deliberations will begin on Monday, August 17.

Suansing said the chamber hopes to pass the House version of the budget by October 9. – Rappler.com

World.title: Quezon City eyes solar power for more public buildings after 25 schools
World.content:
PANELS. 170 solar panels installed on the rooftop of Novaliches High School in Quezon City.

MANILA, Philippines – Twenty-five public schools in Quezon City now use solar panels to help power their daily operations, while the local government is looking to expand the program to more schools and public buildings.

The plan also followed the installation of solar panels on several buildings inside the Quezon City Hall compound. With a working budget of P300 million, the city government expanded this initiative and selected schools. A total of 4,250 solar panels were installed across 25 schools.

According to City Engineer Dale Perral, the budget covered not only solar technology but also rehabilitation work needed to prepare the schools for solar systems. Materials were purchased before prices soared due to the US-Israel war on Iran.

“The school solarization program is a key driver of local climate action,” said Perral.

Among the schools now with solar panels installed are Camp General Emilio Aguinaldo High School, Commonwealth Elementary School, and North Fairview Elementary School.

The city engineer said they have partnered with the C40 Cities – a global network of mayors for climate action – for guidance. But the technology and materials used in the city compound and school buildings were procured through public bidding.

Play Video

Outside Quezon City, more public schools could see solar power projects in the near future.

Education Secretary Sonny Angara earlier said the government is considering installing solar panels on public school rooftops across the country. It could begin by 2027 if funding is allocated, as the agency has no budget for such program this year.

Concerns over energy security have gained renewed urgency amid global oil supply disruptions caused by the US-Iran war. Demand for solar power among Filipino households has surged, raising interest and putting pressure on the local industry to deliver more than it has in the past.

Quezon City is already laying the groundwork that other cities may use as a template in the future. Aside from more schools, the city is also eyeing other public buildings as well.

“[S]ome of our institutional buildings as well, iyong mga public libraries and barangay halls and city government-owned buildings,” said Perral. “Paunti-unti we are installing the same.” (Some of our institutional buildings, the public libraries, village halls, and city government buildings – little by little, we are installing the same).

‘Models of sustainability’

Discussions on solar energy in the Philippines have largely focused on household installations, including how to install solar systems and their cost, as well as large-scale corporate projects.

Local governments can serve as models for sustainability by installing solar systems on city-owned buildings and bringing the shift to solar power closer to communities.

The Department of Energy partnered with Metro Manila cities in 2025 to implement energy-saving projects, including the installation of solar systems on key public buildings.

“Every kilowatt-hour saved in our public facilities translates into more resources for classrooms, health centers, and social services that directly uplift our people,” Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said earlier.

Cities can cut costs by installing solar systems on public buildings, as Quezon City has found after installing solar panels at three city-owned hospitals. The 786 panels are expected to save the city government about P5.5 million a year. – Rappler.com

World.title: At least 19 dead due to storms, monsoon – NDRRMC
World.content:
CLEARING. Rescuers gather in Antipolo City on August 9, to retrieve a delivery rider covered by a fallen tree and utility pole.

At least 7,000 farmers are affected, while 5,000 hectares of farmland, or 85% of the affected area, are unlikely to recover

MANILA, Philippines – At least 19 people died due to the combined effects of the southwest monsoon, Tropical Depression Luis and Tropical Storm Maymay (Kujira), the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council reported Tuesday, August 11.

Twelve of the recorded deaths were in Benguet, due to landslides. Four people died in Rizal and three in Batangas. Fifteen people were injured and four were reported missing. So far, the government has provided P73.5 million in assistance.

Antipolo City reported one fatality, a delivery rider who died after a tree and a Meralco utility pole fell on him. The city government has promised to assist the family through the wake and burial.

Farmers reeling from continuous rain

Meanwhile, the agriculture sector is dealing with at least P197.15 million in production value losses, the Department of Agriculture (DA) reported Tuesday. Areas adversely affected include Ilocos Region, Cagayan, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, Mimaropa, and Western Visayas. Rice farmers were hit the hardest.

The DA was preparing P106.5 million worth of agricultural inputs to help farmers as of Monday, August 10.

“We need our people on the ground to move quickly so affected farmers can get the assistance they need, especially insurance claims and credit support,” Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel said Monday. “The faster we process these, the faster farmers can recover and get back to production.”

At least 7,000 farmers were affected, while 5,000 hectares of farmland, or 85% of the affected area, are unlikely to recover.

The Philippine Space Agency’s mapping on August 6 showed rice farms in La Union and Pangasinan flooded. Agoo, La Union, and Calasiao, Pangasinan also had several flood areas.

MAP. The Philippine Space Agency mapped the extent of flooding in Region 1, August 6. Parts of the region are flooded due to the combined effects of Tropical Storm Maymay and the habagat.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Fewer Births, Better Chances: Kazakhstan Advances in Newborn Care
World.content:
ASTANA —Kazakhstan recorded nearly 150,000 births in the first half of 2026, down approximately 7% year on year, while neonatal mortality fell to 3.9 per 1,000 live births in 2025, the lowest rate in Central Asia, according to the Bureau of National Statistics and the Ministry of Healthcare.

The decline in births follows a broader downward trend in Kazakhstan’s total fertility rate, which measures the average number of children a woman would have over her reproductive years. A demographic review by the Unified Accumulative Pension Fund (UAPF) shows the rate fell from 3.32 children per woman in 2021 to 3.06 in 2022 and 2.57 in 2025. The review described declining fertility as part of a broader global trend.

According to the Bureau of National Statistics, 335,000 children were born in Kazakhstan in 2025, with boys accounting for 51.5% of births and girls for 48.5%. The country recorded 64,700 deaths from January through June, resulting in a natural population increase of 85,100 people.

While the birth rate has been declining, the ministry data show improving outcomes for newborns requiring specialized medical care, particularly premature babies and children born with severe congenital conditions.

Survival improves in complex neonatal cases

Over the past five years, mortality among newborns with severe congenital conditions has fallen more than threefold, from 22% to 6.9%, while postoperative survival has risen to 93%. Approximately 1,400 operations are performed on newborns each year, with specialized care available at perinatal centers across Kazakhstan.

The ministry attributes the improvement to the development of obstetric and neonatal services, the introduction of modern medical technologies and the work of specialized medical teams. Such treatment can be particularly demanding for premature babies, who require specialized preparation before surgery and intensive care afterward.

Neonatal and pediatric surgeon Zhenis Sakuov told The Astana Times that successful treatment depends on coordination across the entire medical team.

“Operating on newborns is difficult, and operating on premature babies is even more difficult because they require specialized preparation for surgery. (…) The operation itself is complex, the postoperative period is complex, and they need specialized care afterward. This is teamwork,” he said.

About 17,000 premature babies were born in Kazakhstan last year, with each receiving a range of specialized medical care, according to the ministry.

Earlier diagnosis expands treatment options

Advances in neonatal care increasingly begin before birth. Modern prenatal diagnostics can detect many congenital conditions between 18 and 20 weeks of pregnancy, allowing doctors to determine how the pregnancy and delivery should be managed and prepare a medical team to assist the child immediately after birth. When fetal abnormalities are identified, expectant mothers are referred to specialized perinatal centers, where doctors determine the timing and method of delivery and prepare a treatment plan in advance.

This approach has also expanded through one-day clinics at fetal health centers. According to the ministry, since their introduction in 2024, prenatal screening coverage has increased by 10%, detection of fetal abnormalities by 12%, and childhood disability has declined by 8%.

Treatment in some cases can now begin even before delivery. Kazakhstan is developing fetal surgery, or the intrauterine correction of certain fetal conditions, with procedures performed at specialized centers in Astana and Almaty.

For some conditions, treatment can begin even before delivery. Kazakhstan is developing fetal surgery, which involves correcting certain fetal conditions in the womb, with procedures performed at specialized centers in Astana and Almaty.

After birth, about one-third of newborn surgeries are now performed using minimally invasive techniques. Kazakhstan has also used extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) since 2022 to support patients in critical condition with severe respiratory failure.

“Intensive care is developing, as well as extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, anesthesiology, and diagnostics. All of this significantly increases children’s chances of recovery and a good quality of life. And most importantly, many families today can receive high-tech medical care without leaving Kazakhstan,” Pediatric Cardiac Surgeon Tlektes Nashkenov told The Astana Times.

The ministry’s data show survival rates of 80% to 90% for children born with congenital diaphragmatic hernia, 85% to 95% for esophageal atresia and more than 90% for gastroschisis. Mortality among premature babies with necrotizing enterocolitis has fallen more than 2.5 times as diagnostic and surgical treatment has improved.

World.title: eGov GPT Expansion Advances Kazakhstan’s Digital Government Push
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan plans to expand its AI-powered eGov GPT assistant so that services available through it account for approximately 70% of citizen requests by the end of 2026, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said at an Aug. 11 government meeting.

The assistant currently provides access to 50 of the most frequently requested government services, which together account for approximately 30% of citizen requests. Since its launch in April, eGov GPT has been used more than 150,000 times. Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov instructed the ministry and government agencies to increase the number of services available through the assistant to 150 by year-end.

The system allows users to describe their situation in ordinary text rather than search for the appropriate form, certificate or government agency. The assistant identifies the relevant service, prepares the required application and provides the result.

“eGov GPT should become a universal AI assistant for all matters involving interaction between the state and citizens,” said Madiyev.

The expansion is part of Kazakhstan’s broader effort to integrate artificial intelligence into public services under the Digital Qazaqstan strategy, approved in June.

“The year of digitalization and artificial intelligence marks the starting point for achieving this goal. In June, the nationwide Digital Qazaqstan strategy was approved, with the digitalization of public services identified as one of its key priorities,” said Bektenov.

The Aug. 11 meeting, chaired by Bektenov, focused on developing an AI-based public service ecosystem and implementing President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s instructions to accelerate digital transformation across the economy and public administration. The government is also seeking to make interactions with citizens and businesses increasingly digital and proactive.

Government agencies shift to QazTech

All government agencies are now working with QazTech, Kazakhstan’s unified platform for developing digital public services, while the migration of existing information systems continues under a two-year government plan. The platform has been operating since April 1 and is designed to shorten the development and launch of new digital services from several years to several weeks.

“This year, 39 systems are scheduled for migration, with work on 36 nearing completion. Another 25 systems are being migrated or developed outside the plan, while 10 systems are already fully operational on the platform. This means the work is progressing ahead of schedule, and today all government agencies are already working with QazTech,” said Madiyev.

A moratorium on creating new government information systems outside QazTech has also been in effect since the beginning of 2026. The move is intended to consolidate digital development within a common technological environment, reduce duplicative systems and establish shared standards across government agencies.

Kazakhstan launches eGov 3.0

The government has also launched eGov 3.0, an upgraded version of Kazakhstan’s electronic government portal built on the QazTech platform.

According to Madiyev, the previous eGov portal had reached the limits of its technological capacity, prompting the launch of eGov 3.0 on the QazTech platform. The upgraded portal simplifies services by removing unnecessary requirements and steps, with several of the most frequently requested services already available in the new format.

The modernization is aimed at simplifying access to public services while reducing pressure on government digital infrastructure as demand for online services continues to grow.

According to the latest United Nations e-government survey published in 2024, Kazakhstan ranks 24th among 193 countries in the E-Government Development Index, with a score of 0.9009, placing it in the UN’s “very high” e-government development group.

World.title: What Lies Behind Kazakhstan’s External Debt
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s external debt rose 7.5% year on year to $182.8 billion as of April 1. External liabilities of the government and state-controlled institutions jumped 39%, while private-sector debt remained virtually unchanged and intercompany debt linked to foreign direct investment declined 5.5% in one year.

The National Bank defines external debt as debt obligations of Kazakhstan’s residents to nonresidents. The measure covers both public- and private-sector liabilities and includes debt regardless of the currency in which it is denominated.

From April 1, 2025 to April 1, 2026, gross external debt increased from $170 billion to $182.8 billion, up $12.8 billion, or 7.5%. Intercompany debt linked to foreign direct investment fell from $92.5 billion to $87.4 billion, a decline of 5.5%. As of April, $19.2 billion was owed by banks, an increase from $14.6 billion a year earlier.

Public external debt rose from $14.7 to $18.9 billion in a year. The figures show that most of Kazakhstan’s external liabilities remain outside the government balance sheet. The latest National Bank data points to sovereign and state-controlled borrowers accounting for a growing share of the increase since the start of 2025.

Kazakhstan’s external debt is predominantly long term, with 87.1% carrying an original maturity of more than one year. According to the National Bank, that limits immediate liquidity pressure, but it does not remove longer-term risks, as refinancing and servicing costs can rise when global financial conditions tighten. Loans and borrowings from nonresidents make up 69.2% of the total, while debt securities held by foreign investors account for 13%.

By creditor jurisdiction, the Netherlands accounted for the largest share of Kazakhstan’s external debt as of April 1, at approximately $40.8 billion, followed by the United Kingdom at $19.8 billion, Russia at $16.7 billion, China at $13.8 billion and the United States at $11 billion.

The figures should not be interpreted as direct bilateral government lending, however, as they include corporate and intercompany liabilities and may reflect the jurisdiction through which financial claims are held or administered. In the case of the Netherlands, data from the National Bank shows that of $41 billion total, government debt is only $21 million, banks – $11 million and intercompany debt – $38.23 billion, so roughly 94% of Kazakhstan’s debt recorded against the Netherlands is intercompany FDI debt.

External debt of Central Asian countries excluding Turkmenistan increased by 34.9% over the past five years, reaching nearly $290.8 billion in 2025, according to data from the CIS Statistical Committee and the Eurasian Economic Commission. Kazakhstan accounted for 62.5% of the total.

Despite having by far the largest external debt stock in Central Asia, Kazakhstan’s general government debt burden remains comparatively moderate. The International Monetary Fund data put general government gross debt at around 24.9% of GDP, compared with 27.5% in Uzbekistan and 37.4% in Kyrgyzstan.

The size of the debt, however, is only one measure of fiscal vulnerability. Economists also look at the cost of servicing it, its currency and maturity structure, and how borrowed funds are used. A country with a relatively high debt ratio can remain financially stable if investors retain confidence and debt-service costs remain manageable.

World.title: New Security Architecture: Future of Abraham Accords and  Emerging Strategic Landscape for Kazakhstan
World.content:
On July 22, Washington hosted an important hearing of the U.S. House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on the Middle East and North Africa, titled “Building a New Regional Security Architecture: The Next Phase of the Abraham Accords.” American lawmakers, diplomats, and experts, including Daniel Shapiro, former U.S. Ambassador to Israel, gathered at the Capitol to discuss the broader transformation of the framework under the auspices of the White House.

The hearing, together with the current geopolitical agenda, made one trend increasingly clear: the Abraham Accords have moved decisively beyond the confines of the Middle East and are evolving into a broader international coalition, with Kazakhstan assuming an important precedent-setting role.

The discussions in Congress provide valuable insight into the key trends likely to shape the future development of the Accords and help define Astana’s place within this emerging international architecture.

Resetting the framework: From a regional pact to a “Club of Power”

Speakers before Congress emphasized that the Abraham Accords have demonstrated their resilience even under the most difficult circumstances following the October 2023 crisis. The current strategy of the Donald Trump administration rests on two major pillars.

The U.S.-Saudi Nuclear Deal

The long-anticipated agreement on civilian nuclear cooperation between Washington and Riyadh has now been concluded. On July 22, U.S. Secretary of Energy Chris Wright and Saudi Minister of Energy Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed an agreement establishing a framework for long-term cooperation on the peaceful uses of nuclear energy.

The significance of the agreement extends well beyond the energy sector. It represents an important element of the broader U.S. strategy to build a new regional architecture in which economic integration, advanced technology, energy cooperation, and security partnerships increasingly complement the normalization process associated with the Abraham Accords.

At the same time, the nuclear agreement should be viewed separately from the question of Saudi-Israeli normalization. While normalization remains an important strategic objective for Washington, the two tracks are not identical. The conclusion of the nuclear agreement nevertheless strengthens the broader strategic framework within which future regional arrangements may develop.

Expanding the Geographic Scope

The second pillar is the expansion of the Accords beyond their original Middle Eastern framework. Bringing influential states from outside the Arab world into the process demonstrates that the platform can serve as a broader mechanism for international cooperation, reinforcing its relevance, resilience, and legitimacy.

The Central Asian dimension: why do the Accords matter for Kazakhstan?

Kazakhstan’s formal accession to the Abraham Accords in November 2025 was highlighted at the congressional hearing as an important diplomatic precedent. Daniel Shapiro, former U.S. Ambassador to Israel and a prominent American expert on the regional normalization process,emphasized in his testimony that Kazakhstan’s decision helped dispel skepticism about the framework and demonstrated its appeal beyond the Arab world, particularly among moderate Muslim-majority states.

Against the backdrop of today’s geopolitical turbulence, participation in the Accords offers Kazakhstan three strategic opportunities.

Diplomatic Balancing and Multi-Vector Foreign Policy

Positioned at the intersection of Russian and Chinese interests, Astana can use the platform as an additional instrument for diversifying its international partnerships. This allows Kazakhstan to broaden its network of strategic partners without entering into direct confrontation with regional powers or Tehran.

At the same time, Kazakhstan’s engagement with the Abraham Accords should not be interpreted as a departure from its traditional multi-vector foreign policy. Rather, it reflects an adaptation of that policy to a rapidly changing global environment.

Experts increasingly point to a shift from a largely passive model of maneuvering between major powers toward a more active model of pragmatic and sovereign balancing, in which foreign policy is increasingly anchored in the protection of national interests and economic security.

Under this approach, diversification is not an end in itself. It is a strategic instrument designed to preserve Kazakhstan’s sovereignty, expand its room for maneuver, reduce excessive dependence on any single external partner, and secure access to capital, technology, markets, and critical infrastructure.

Participation in the Abraham Accords therefore fits within the broader evolution of Kazakhstan’s foreign policy: not a rejection of multi-vector diplomacy, but its modernization in response to a more fragmented, competitive, and unpredictable international system.

A Direct Track to Washington

Demonstrating support for U.S.-backed peace and normalization initiatives can strengthen Kazakhstan’s standing in Washington. This is particularly important for safeguarding long-term American investment in Kazakhstan’s energy sector and critical minerals, while also helping the country navigate the risks created by global tariff disputes and geopolitical fragmentation.

For Astana, closer engagement with the United States through emerging regional frameworks can therefore serve both diplomatic and economic purposes. It creates an additional channel for dialogue with Washington while reinforcing Kazakhstan’s broader strategy of maintaining diversified external partnerships.

A Pragmatic Economic Foundation

The expanding framework can provide Astana with access to new sources of capital and technology. Wealthy Gulf states, particularly the United Arab Emirates, can contribute financing to major infrastructure and connectivity projects, while Israel offers advanced expertise in areas such as cybersecurity, artificial intelligence, water management, agricultural technology, and resource efficiency.

For Kazakhstan, therefore, the value of the Accords lies not simply in diplomatic symbolism. Their importance increasingly rests on the possibility of connecting different pools of capital, technology, infrastructure, and political influence within a broader international framework.

At the same time, as experts at the hearing made clear, Kazakhstan retains its sovereign position. Participation in the Accords does not alter Astana’s commitment to a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict or its support for humanitarian efforts. Kazakhstan can therefore participate in the emerging framework while maintaining its established position on the Palestinian issue.

The future of the Abraham Accords lies in their transformation from a primarily regional political and security framework into a broader international network encompassing security, connectivity, logistics, energy, investment, and technological cooperation under U.S. leadership.

The developments of 2026 suggest that this transformation is already underway. The expansion of the Accords beyond the Arab world, Kazakhstan’s participation, and the newly concluded U.S.-Saudi nuclear cooperation agreement all point toward an emerging architecture that is considerably broader than the original normalization framework.

For Kazakhstan, the Abraham Accords are therefore becoming more than a symbolic diplomatic gesture. They represent an additional instrument of the country’s long-standing multi-vector foreign policy — one that can help Astana diversify strategic partnerships, attract new investment and technology, deepen its engagement with Washington and the Gulf states, and strengthen its resilience amid growing geopolitical competition.

The strategic opportunity for Kazakhstan lies in turning its early participation into practical cooperation — transforming diplomatic positioning into tangible economic benefits, technological partnerships, and greater geopolitical resilience.

The author is Sapargali Shalgimbayev, the president of the CFive Intellectual Platform, an independent think tank based at Astana International University.
