World.title: How Spider-Man: Brand New Day side-stepped the superhero slump
World.content:
CultureMoviesMarvel How Spider-Man: Brand New Day side-stepped the superhero slump Nell Geraets August 11, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Anyone with even the slightest Spidey sense knew Spider-Man: Brand New Day would do well at the box office. The three previous Tom Holland-led films were warmly received, and its record-breaking trailer drop in March sent superhero fans into a frenzy. But the movie didn’t just do well at the box office, it absolutely smashed it. Destin Daniel Cretton’s film enjoyed the best US domestic opening weekend ever, grossing $US360 ($510) million, and beating 2019’s previous heavy-hitter, Avengers: Endgame ($US357 million). After just over a week in cinemas, it had already surpassed $US1 billion globally. Spider-Man: Brand New Day has exploded at the box office. Sony Pictures In Australia, the movie recorded the biggest opening weekend of the year, surpassing Disney’s Toy Story 5. It grossed $30.43 million on its opening weekend – the second-best result ever, behind only Avengers: Endgame’s $34.1 million. These results are even more impressive against the current state of superhero fare. According to data from the FranchiseRe industry newsletter, annual box office revenue for superhero movies is down by an average of $US3.5 billion, about half of the pre-pandemic peak from 2017-19.



Related Article Cinema Have Tom Holland and Zendaya just saved the cinema business? Audiences are fatigued by capes, spandex and multiverses, whether that’s because of the sheer overload of content, or perhaps due to new C and D-list superheroes taking over screens. Brand New Day, however, appears to have beaten these odds, generating major excitement around a genre that has fallen flat. So, how has Spidey overcome the superhero slump? No ensemble? Yes, please The superhero genre loves an ensemble. This only intensified when Avengers: Infinity War smashed the box office in 2018, triggering a slew of multi-hero Marvel titles such as Eternals, Thunderbolts*, The Fantastic Four: First Steps, and DC’s The Suicide Squad and Zack Snyder’s Justice League. Even the previous Spider-Man film, No Way Home, featured something of a “semi-ensemble”, pulling in previous Spideys Tobey Maguire and Andrew Garfield.



Brand New Day, however, drew it way back. The sole focus is on Peter Parker – after all, the world no longer remembers him, ridding him of his trusted mentors and pals, and giving him little choice but to propel the film largely on his own. Stripping a superhero film back to a sole protagonist – an extremely isolated one, at that – creates space to understand Parker’s internal turmoil and his deep longing for connection, feelings most of us can relate to, especially post-pandemic. Loading With less multiverse madness, the film remains entirely character-driven. In fact, chairman and CEO of Sony Pictures Entertainment Motion Picture Group, Tom Rothman, told The Los Angeles Times the film is about a “superperson” rather than a “superhero”. And Spider-Man was arguably the ideal superperson in which to invest. Since first appearing on screen in an animated TV series in 1967, he’s proven to be a lucrative character, attracting not only comic book fans (the first comic book appearance was in 1962), but also casual movie-goers and even families (all live-action Spider-Man feature films are internationally rated PG-13). Having attained his arachnid powers while still in high school, Parker brings a youthful energy to what can sometimes be a grim genre. His is ultimately a coming-of-age story, a narrative-style that has demonstrated time again to work across all four quadrants.



From Tobey Maguire to Tom Holland, Spider-Man has been a super popular hero for decades. Zade Rosenthal Back to basics Brand New Day hasn’t just stripped back the characters. The entire film returns to Spider-Man’s street-level roots, focusing on New York City’s more localised crime rather than world-ending chaos. He’s our friendly neighbourhood Spider-Man, after all. This hearkens back to earlier, pre-MCU titles, such as Blade (1998), which grounded itself in a gritty urban environment where underground crime syndicates posed the biggest threat. Its visual style feels more grounded, too. Cretton, who helmed Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings and Wonder Man, consciously chose to shoot on location, including in Glasgow and a UK prison. View post on X



He also opted against an overload of CGI, which has become the norm for most superhero fare (looking at you, Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania). Instead, much of Brand New Day is executed practically, such as the fully functional subway car built especially for the movie, as well as Holland’s largely unenhanced physical stunts. Given concerns around AI and the excitement for directors like Christopher Nolan using practical effects, it’s clear audiences increasingly yearn to see the actual craft behind movie-making alongside a killer story. No homework required Related Article DC Universe Supergirl is tanking at the box office ... but it isn’t the heroine’s fault One of the main gripes superhero fans have these days is the overload of content. To understand an upcoming film, there’s a massive backlog of other movies and TV shows you need to watch first. In Brand New Day’s case, however, there’s very little to catch up on. Sure, there are three previous Holland-led titles (Homecoming, Far From Home and No Way Home), but Marvel gave us a solid four-year break after the previous instalment. That’s ample catch-up time for even for the busiest fans.



In fact, you don’t even really need to have seen the first three films. No one remembers Parker in Brand New Day, meaning the slate is wiped almost entirely clean. Some may wish to familiarise themselves with certain Marvel properties such as Damage Control or The Punisher, but beyond that, the film largely stands on its own. Tom Holland mania He acts, dances, does acrobatics – he’s even known to dabble in woodwork. Tom Holland has come into his own recently, impressing audiences with his talent range and genuinely likeable off-screen charm. His penchant for high-fiving kids on red carpets and teasing himself in interviews gels well with fans, and makes his turn as Spider-Man – a character known for youthful innocence – even more believable. Tom Holland can act, dance, and even carve wood. Now, he can add smashing the box office to that list. He exudes so much talent that he’s even been cast to embody Fred Astaire in Paul King’s upcoming biopic about the debonair dancer. This casting is off the back of a blockbuster season for Holland, who has just completed promotional tours for Nolan’s The Odyssey and Brand New Day, each very different films that have both stormed the box office. It is suggested his range and ability to command attention on the big screen could send him on a similar trajectory as other A-list stars like Daniel Radcliffe, Robert Pattinson or even Tom Cruise.

World.title: Josh Fraser enters the Carlton coaching race after stunning on-field turnaround
World.content:
In today’s AFL Briefing, your wrap of footy news: Interim Carlton coach Josh Fraser will throw his hat in the ring for the full-time role.

Former Melbourne skipper Jack Viney is preparing for his long-awaited return from injury.

Nick Larkey has opened up on his goal-kicking troubles. Interim Carlton coach Josh Fraser will present for the club’s vacant coaching position after accepting an invitation to join the process. The Blues have won 10 of their 12 games under Fraser since he took over as interim when Michael Voss departed after the club won just one out of their first nine matches for the season. Josh Fraser will be a contender for the Carlton coaching role after all. Getty Images Fraser said he would not be a candidate for the full-time position when he accepted the interim role, but recognised in recent weeks he needed to give it serious consideration as the Blues showed extraordinary form under his leadership.



According to two competition sources, speaking on condition of anonymity, Fraser has communicated his decision to take part in the process. The Blues now sit inside the top 10, and with two games remaining are in a good position to at least reach the wildcard finals round. The club invited Fraser to be part of the process about a fortnight ago and the 44-year-old said he needed time to consider whether the timing was right. He then delayed his decision further after his father Bill died on July 30, with the funeral held on Monday. Fremantle’s Jaymie Graham, Hawthorn’s Daniel Giansiracusa, Geelong’s James Kelly and St Kilda’s Corey Enright are already on the club’s shortlist, with the Blues adamant a selection process is still required to determine the best candidate to take the club forward.



Fraser has been determined to make sure the club could keep the performance of the team for the remainder of 2026 separate to the coaching search, which is being led by CEO Graham Wright and football boss Chris Davies. Related Article AFL 2026 The two teams with a sneaky chance to snatch a wildcard The Blues face the Western Bulldogs and top-of-the-ladder Fremantle in the final two rounds of the home-and-away season, with one win needed to guarantee them a spot in the wildcard round after they knocked off St Kilda and the Brisbane Lions in the past two games. Essendon are also yet to fill their vacant coaching position, with their selection panel considering Sydney’s Mark McVeigh, Graham, Adelaide’s Murray Davis and Bombers great and former coach (current Port Melbourne coaching director) James Hird to fill the spot. Interim Bombers coach Dean Solomon, a former teammate of both Hird and McVeigh, has ruled himself out of the process.

- Peter Ryan Demons welcome back a favourite son



Oliver Caffrey Melbourne vice captain Jack Viney will play his first game in almost a year as he tries to be part of the surging Demons’ finals campaign. Having dealt with complex back and Achilles injuries, Viney hasn’t played a match at any level this season. After a month of training Jack Viney is set to make his return to the playing field in Melbourne’s VFL team this weekend. Getty Images The strong-bodied midfielder’s most recent game was Melbourne’s round 24 loss to Collingwood last August, before Steven King took over as Demons coach.



But the premiership hero will return via the VFL on Sunday when the Casey Demons face Box Hill. “He’s been full training now for nearly a month ... so we finally get a game into him,” King said on Tuesday. “He’s obviously chomping at the bit, vice captain of our footy club and the ultimate competitor and the type of player you want to run out with. Loading “We’ve got to make sure that we do what’s right for Jack and right for the footy club.



“But if he can get through that game, then he’ll put his name up in lights and make himself available and see what happens from there.” After a stunning four-point win over premiership favourites Fremantle last Saturday, Melbourne locked in their finals spot. Having an experienced player like Viney slot into a September campaign makes the Demons a dangerous prospect. Viney stretches out at training. Getty Images But King has cautioned against expecting too much from the 32-year-old.



“We have to respect what he’s been through,” King said of Viney. “But I feel like you can’t just get given a game on reputation and your standing. “The first thing is just to get through a whole competitive game, and make sure he pulls up OK. “I want him to actually make sure of the long term as well and that he leaves this year well, ready for next season.”



Complicating any AFL return for Viney, Casey’s VFL campaign will come to an end this Sunday as they have not qualified for finals. King expressed his frustration at the inconsistent scheduling of the VFL, with numerous byes during the season making it hard for reserves players to build momentum. Related Article AFL 2026 Emails between Cats, AFL at the centre of club’s Kolodjashnij defence “We’ve got professional athletes that need to play games and develop, and that’s what I feel like the VFL competition is for – it’s for us to develop young men to play and be ready to play AFL,” King said.



“For every week they have off, that’s a missed opportunity where they get to develop and grow and learn. “It’s something I feel like the AFL certainly needs to look at aligning the seasons.” Youngster Latrelle Pickett will also return via the VFL this weekend after recovering from a concussion. Pickett was spoken to by Demons leaders after consuming alcohol days after suffering the head knock in a defeat to Geelong three weeks ago. King called the counselling of Pickett a “non-story”.



The Demons this week confirmed the impending retirement of their football manager Alan Richardson, as foreshadowed by this masthead last week. It ends a four-decade career in the AFL for the former Collingwood player and St Kilda coach.

- AAP North skipper discusses his yips in front of goal Scott Spits North Melbourne skipper Nick Larkey admitted he’s been battling the yips after returning 39.27 in front of goal so far this season. In comparison, three years ago, he booted 71 goals – getting within sight of the Coleman Medal won by Charlie Curnow – and snagged a combined 87.29 across seasons 2024 and 2025.



Kangaroos skipper Nick Larkey has opened up on his set-shot troubles. Getty Images “It’s been challenging,” Larkey said at North’s Arden Street base on Tuesday. “It’s been something that’s so strong in my game, and it’s held me in good stead for my career.” Larkey spoke about his frustration at watching his goal kicking “drop away”. “For it to drop away ... I’ve always really prided myself on being able to finish off the work for the team,” he said.



“We do a hell of a work to get the ball there, and it’s my job to finish the goals. “For a six-game period there, they just weren’t going through. It’s tough navigating your way through it, because you don’t want to over-think it, but then when everyone’s got suggestions on how you’re going to fix it, you sort of adjust little things here and there. “Is it technique? Is it a handling the moment thing? Is it being present? It’s a combination of things. “What I have been happy with myself about is my ability to work through it. I think I’ve become a lot mentally stronger, and more resilient, and more present with the way I handle those situations. “It doesn’t guarantee I’m going to kick everything through the middle. No player in history has. But it’s a matter of handling those moments better, and trusting a good routine.



“And [it’s] also a lot of repetition at training. I’ve got a commitment for the end of the year to have as many shots that I possibly can.” Larkey said the Roos still have plenty to play for in 2026, as they cling to a “mathematical” chance of reaching the AFL’s wildcard round. And there’s also the chance ahead of them to defeat Geelong for the first time in 11 years when the two clubs clash at Marvel Stadium as part of an AFL/AFLW double-header on Saturday. North Melbourne star Ash Riddell is the reigning AFLW best and fairest. AFL Photos The Kangaroos have improved considerably this year, holding a 9-12 record to sit two games and percentage outside the top 10. They’ll have to rely on Carlton falling at the final hurdle to snatch the last spot in the AFL’s rejigged finals format. North haven’t extended their season beyond home-and-away games since 2016.



“I don’t think I’ve ever beaten the Cats – VFL or AFL – in my time,” said the 28-year-old Larkey. “The teams we’re playing are really quality opposition, Geelong [and] Sydney. “We came really close to the Swans, and we held the Cats for three quarters last time we played them. And we’ve improved a lot since then. “Our footy as it’s best, we’ve got the belief that it could beat anyone. It’s just a matter of doing it consistently for as long as possible.” In the last contest between the teams, Geelong won by 49 points at GMHBA Stadium in early May, thanks in part to a nine-goal final quarter as the Kangas fell away.



“We were really good in the contest,” recalled first-year captain Larkey. “The midfield got on top for three quarters, and then the Cats threw a few changes around the ball, and I don’t think we adjusted as well as we could have. “Their running power it felt like on the day took over in the fourth [quarter]. We just fell away. “Geelong historically have been really good at adjusting, adapting when things aren’t working. So we’ll be better prepared for that this week.” North AFLW star Ash Riddell said the chance to unfurl the club’s latest premiership flag in front of a bumper Marvel crowd will be “really special”.



“Crock [coach Darren Crocker] always talks about enjoying the journey, so it’s something that we’ll look at and be really proud of,” said Riddell as the Roos look to extend their 27-match winning streak and chase a hat-trick of AFLW premierships. “Obviously knowing this is a new season, we’re pretty eager to get stuck into things. “Well move on pretty quick after that.” Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Forget big lips and frozen foreheads: the new home of ‘natural beauty’
World.content:
LifestyleBeautyTrends Forget big lips and frozen foreheads: the new home of ‘natural beauty’ Damien Woolnough August 11, 2026 — 6:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cosmetic physician Dr Joseph Hkeik’s clientele includes supermodels, singers and socialites but the latest patient to experience his powers of transformation is a sprawling 145-year-old Victorian villa on Sydney’s North Shore. The former home, library and restaurant Boronia House has been transformed into a temple of self-improvement with the same level of care that Hkeik’s staff at his All Saints clinics exercise to treat the faces of Elle Macpherson, Miranda Kerr, Rita Ora and Eva Mendes. Dr Joseph Hkeik inside All Saints new home in Mosman, reimagined by interior architect Blainey North. KATE GERAGHTY “I was looking for a smaller version of All Saints in Double Bay,” says Hkeik, referring to his Eastern Suburbs flagship which has become part of the itinerary for international celebrities passing through Sydney. There are also outposts in North Parramatta and Balmain. “I came to look at something in this area, walked by, and it was love at first sight.”



Hkeik is used to dealing with before photos, and so he could see the building’s beauty was lurking beneath years of disrepair. A different kind of filler than the one used in his clinics was required, so an urgent phone call was placed to frequent collaborator interior architect Blainey North who has shaped the homes of A-list Australian clients including Nicole Kidman, Russell Crowe and the Packer and Pratt families. Related Article Opinion

Nutrition Is there lead in your coffee and parasites in your sushi? Miranda Kerr’s ‘comical’ diet Sarah Berry Lifestyle Health Editor The building’s refresh took longer than the average two-hour visit to All Saints. “It has been nearly four years since I first saw it,” Hkeik says. “I don’t rush because I think that when you rush, you make compromises.” With Le Petit Saint in Mayfair, London, which opened in 2020, Hkeik has built an empire around a specific approach to beauty that is the antithesis of the exaggerated lips, frozen foreheads and overly sculpted cheeks of corner shop competitors.



The All Saints Clinic in Mosman. KATE GERAGHTY When the baronial doors of Boronia house open, Hkeik is not expecting clients to rush inside from their Range Rovers clutching pictures of Kris Jenner for inspiration. “From when I started 27 years ago to now, you’ve seen these people go through the high cheekbones, the big lips, the big everything, that exaggerated look,” Hkeik says. “And now everyone’s just actually begging for that natural look. “We’ve always stuck to the same philosophy and I think this is why we’re still standing. “In the beginning I became unpopular because people were saying, ‘I look better, but no one can tell I’ve done some work’. I couldn’t understand that. Why would you want people to know?



“You should look as if this is how you wake up. This is how you always looked.” While injectables constitute the largest portion of the All Saints business in Double Bay, the new Mosman premises will include more services tapping into a holistic approach to looking and feeling good. On arrival, guests can drown sorrows with wellness elixirs from a tonic bar in the waiting room. For Hkeik, the first treatment is the building itself. “We know that when you’re in love, your skin’s in much better condition. This was made with love.” Make the most of your health with our Live Well newsletter. Get it in your inbox every Monday.

World.title: AI is cutting graduate jobs. These are the skills young people will need
World.content:
Exclusive NationalGraduates AI is cutting graduate jobs. These are the skills young people will need Sally Rawsthorne August 11, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Noah Ross Grundmann finishes his accounting degree and steps into full-time work, he knows his future bosses won’t be looking for an AI newbie. “Students need to graduate understanding how AI applies to real workplaces and where compliance, data privacy, accuracy and human accountability actually matter,” said the 20-year-old, who also works as a finance and compliance officer at a not-for-profit. “AI has probably forced universities to think carefully about how they assess learning,” said Noah Ross Grundmann. Ruby Alexander AI expertise has become increasingly crucial for university leavers’ job prospects yet it is a double-edged sword. The technology is so capable that it could wipe out half of all white-collar entry-level jobs, says Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, which built AI assistant Claude, while the World Economic Forum predicts that 39 per cent of jobs will “fundamentally change” by 2030. Those predictions are being realised already. Law firm MinterEllison in May announced it was cutting its graduate intake from more than 100 to 72, The Australian Financial Review reported.



“Responsible use of AI is improving efficiency in some of the more routine work graduates traditionally start on, while demand continues to shift towards complex matters,” MinterEllison chief people officer Rachel Banks said. “That combination has led us to take a more targeted approach.” Related Article University Study company helping Australian university students cheat sued in landmark court case Other law firms said their reduced graduate hire was not because of AI but a reflection of the wider labour market. Changes are also afoot in accounting. At PricewaterhouseCoopers, AI has changed the Australian graduate hiring pattern. The firm has cut entry-level roles by 6 per cent, while it is looking for half of its 2027 graduate intake to come from non-accounting backgrounds. Deloitte hired 655 university leavers this year (down from 730 last year), with “strong demand” for technology, data and engineering graduates. Morgan Stanley’s US-based AI disruption tracker found that while the technology has not harmed the job market too much, younger workers bear the greatest impact.



“Entry-level roles, which have historically served as the training ground for graduates, are increasingly being reshaped or removed altogether as AI takes on routine cognitive tasks,” said business trend forecaster Michael McQueen. “It’s almost as if the first few rungs of the career ladder are being removed in a number of white-collar professions.” Related Article University ‘AI is insidious’: Universities urged to adopt clear AI rules after opinion article scandal He said the short-term outlook was “more competitive and uncertain” due to the cooling labour market, employers looking to AI for tasks previously done by junior workers, and growing scepticism about the value of a degree as education costs rise. “In the next 12 to 24 months we are likely to see a tougher transition from study to work, particularly for those relying on traditional pathways.” Students and employers alike want universities to move away from policing AI and towards teaching AI skills for the workplace.



“AI literacy is rapidly becoming a core workforce capability. This means teaching students how to critically evaluate outputs and apply them strategically and ethically,” RMIT Online director of customer success Anshu Arora said. “Young workers are particularly vulnerable. Gen Z are twice as likely to overstate their AI skills compared to Baby Boomers, which increases the risk of misuse if they are not equipped with strong critical evaluation skills.” The Future Skills Organisation said employers report graduates are starting work lacking practical skills, AI know-how, communication ability and professional judgment. “As a result, employers are bearing the cost of developing workforce readiness post-hire. This takes away employer investment from early career development for graduates,” it said in a submission to the Australian University Graduates Senate inquiry. Beyond AI skills, McQueen said graduates could stand out in a difficult market if they “double down on the human skills that are harder to automate, such as communication, curiosity, creativity, ethical reasoning and collaboration”. World.title: Scientists scanned 14 canine brains. They found another reason to love dogs
World.content:
NationalPets Scientists scanned 14 canine brains. They found another reason to love dogs Angus Dalton August 11, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

We have a lot of scientifically dodgy beliefs when it comes to our dogs. The idea of needing to show a dog you’re the “alpha” is based on flawed science; they don’t actually see in black and white; and the concept of “dog years” – where one human year equates to seven years in a dog’s life – is a myth. But a new brain-scanning study has revealed new insights into something most dog lovers know to be true: our canine companions are excellent at reading and responding to human emotion. Fourteen dog brains were scanned in MRI machines to see how they reacted to human emotions. Laura V. Cuaya They can tell when we’re happy or sad, and are better at distinguishing between negative emotions such as fear, sadness and anger than we thought. Dogs can read us even better than chimpanzees, our closest evolutionary relatives, the authors claim.



In particular, dog brains light up at happy human faces; even smiles from strangers activate the same region of a dog’s brain that responds to rewards such as toys and treats. Matt Golding Here’s how researchers pinpointed what’s going on inside the brains of our canine companions, and why science says we must smile at every dog we meet (just in case you weren’t doing that already). What a human smile does to a dog’s brain The study was undertaken in Hungary and Mexico. Researchers Dr Raul Hernandez-Perez and Dr Laura Cuaya scouted parks for dogs who seemed calm and well trained, and approached their owners to recruit them for the study.



They gathered a group of 14 dogs, made up of border collies (including the researchers’ own dogs, Odin and Kun-kun), golden retrievers, a labrador and a mutt. Then came the hard part. Even humans find MRIs freaky. How would dogs fare in the clanky, clamorous cylinders, much less stay still enough for the test? Moving just three millimetres during a scan would render the data useless. Two of the new study’s participants, Odin and Kun-kun, check out their own brain scans. Laura V. Cuaya Over 20 training sessions, the researchers painstakingly trained the dogs to lie still in the chamber, in a sphinx position with their jaws on a chin rest, rewarding them with treats and play for lying still. They gradually built from five seconds of stillness to the full three minutes, and introduced special earmuffs to protect the dogs’ hearing.



Training complete, the dogs were scanned while researchers showed them images of human faces that were happy, sad, angry, fearful or neutral. Happy human faces triggered activity in the temporal cortex, an area of the brain that recognises faces and processes emotional cues, and the caudate nucleus, which handles rewards and motivation. “The activity in the caudate nucleus is particularly interesting,” Cuaya, from the University of Vienna, said on the release of the research. “It suggests that happy human faces may have emotional significance for dogs.” ‘We should smile at the dogs – even at random dogs in the street.’ Laura Cuaya, University of Vienna Fear and sadness, on the other hand, activated a different region of the brain called the right rostral suprasylvian gyrus (which processes visual and other sensory information), while anger lit up different sections called the right ectosylvian gyrus and the left splenial gyrus.



Jargon aside, the results show dogs react uniquely to happiness and provide the first evidence dogs can tell the difference between some negative facial expressions (although they didn’t seem to distinguish well between sad and angry faces). Taken together with other studies, one of the main takeaways is that dogs interpret human happiness – even the smiles of strangers – as a reward. Happiness sparked a particularly strong response in dogs’ reward centre of the brain. Dr Laura Cuaya “We can reward our dogs with treats but also reward them with happiness,” Cuaya told the BBC. “So we should smile at the dogs – even at random dogs in the street.” One key tip to give your dog a good life



Animal welfare scientist and dog expert Dr Mia Cobb, who wasn’t involved in the study published in iScience, said the sample size was small but offered valuable proof-of-concept findings that could be tested on other breeds. Related Article Science These popular dogs can’t breathe or give birth properly. Why do we breed them? She said the dogs in the study responded stronger to fear and anger over sadness. “If we’re feeling scared or angry it is really valuable for a dog to pay attention to that,” Cobb, from the University of Melbourne, says. If a person is scared, it could signal to a dog there’s danger nearby, while an angry person might pose a direct threat to a dog. “If we’re feeling sad it’s less relevant for the dog because it’s probably not going to threaten their safety.”



While the study tested dogs’ reactions to still images, in reality they respond to a range of cues, including our tone of voice, body language and, crucially, smell. “There’s been emerging evidence over the last couple of years that really shows dogs are very responsive to things like the odour of fear or odour of anxiety,” Cobb says. On that point, one of the best things we can do for our dogs’ welfare (besides smiling at them) is slowing down on walks and letting them sniff. A good whiff of a funky patch of grass is the dog equivalent of taking in a stunning mountain view, Cobb says. Dr Mia Cobb expertly demonstrates the result of smiling at dogs. Dr Mia Cobb “They really live in a smell-based world, so letting them stop and sniff that tree trunk or wooden post that everyone else has peed on today is actually really important to them living a good life.”



Dr Tiffani Howell, a senior research fellow at La Trobe University, says the results should prompt us to better understand our pets. “Dogs are great at reading us but we’re not great at really reading them,” she says. Take the stereotypical, slinking, “guilty” look you might get after a dog tears up a toilet roll or destroys a shoe. Research shows the dogs are not really feeling guilty – it’s more likely they just know their owner is angry, and act submissive to avoid punishment. A few studies do, however, suggest our pups can experience jealousy when we pat or play with other dogs. New research shows more modern breeds have changes in their brain that aid communication with people. iStock In another just-published study on dog brains, researchers analysed ancient dog breeds (the Samoyed, the New Guinea singing dog, and the African and Korean village dog) and compared them with modern breeds (border collies, labradors and German shepherds).



Thousands of years of artificial selection has rewired the communication-related networks in the brains of modern dogs, boosting their capacity to process words and vocal cues from humans, the researchers reported. “We’ve lived very closely together for a really long time, and nowadays, dogs are reliant on humans for pretty much everything,” Howell, who wasn’t involved in either study, says. “It makes total sense that they would learn to read us very well.” The Examine newsletter explains and analyses science with a rigorous focus on the evidence. Sign up to get it each week.

World.title: Want intimate conversations with strangers in the night? Walk this way
World.content:
CultureTheatreStage Want intimate conversations with strangers in the night? Walk this way Kerrie O'Brien August 11, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A man about to have his leg amputated. A new father singing to his four-day-old baby. A jet-lagged aid worker fresh back from Yemen. A woman, the night her mum died, wanting to thank the nurses for their care. These were all callers to The Nightline, a project created by Roslyn Oades with sound artist Bob Scott, which opens at the Malthouse Theatre next week. Roslyn Oades says her show The Nightline provides a fascinating insight into Melburnians. Jason South At the show, each audience member has a rotary dial telephone and a metal panel with eight channels in it, like an old-fashioned phone operator’s switchboard. You can choose your own adventure, Oades says. “If someone’s talking ... you can disconnect at any point and connect to someone else.” She notes that the now obsolete rotary phones are far more conducive to listening than smartphones, the way their handle curves under your chin and the earpiece to your ear.



As well as the intimate call coming through the phone, the show features Scott’s additional layer of surround sound. It might feature a cluster of voices stating the time of night, a chorus of deep sighs and laughs or the sound of a giant storm coming in. Roslyn Oades, documentary theatre maker. Jason South Oades sees nighttime as a world unto itself and is a regular visitor to it herself. “I’ve had issues with sleep since I was a teenager and continue to have patches where I have a very busy mind and kind of lock into being more of a night person than a day person,” she says. “I went through a period of walking at night and there’s something about looking at the city lights at 3am or 4am. There are just a few lights on, like little lighthouses across the cityscape.” She always wondered who else might be awake and what they might be doing. “The idea was born for this concept of how could I create an experience where we could just dip into all those windows and eavesdrop on those worlds,” she says.



About eight years ago, she decided to capture their experiences, setting up a dedicated phone line and getting the word out. Since then, she has had a few breaks but still looks forward to receiving new messages each morning. People of the night are “an elusive breed” and largely invisible, she says. The best strategy for reaching them is via late-night radio, so she befriended several late-night radio hosts who helped let listeners know about the project. Melbourne is an entirely different world at night time. Joe Armao Oades divides the callers into the visitors – insomniacs who can’t sleep, those whose minds won’t stop ticking over, those on a deadline – and those for whom the night is their natural habitat. “It’s a time for soul-searching for the visitors, and then for the people of the night, it’s like [an] alternative universe that they inhabit,” she says. The Melbourne edition has been six years in the making. Originally commissioned by Rising in 2021, the show – and famously, the entire festival – was cancelled on opening night. Since then, it has travelled to the Sydney Festival, Adelaide Festival, Bleach Festival on the Gold Coast and to Canada. The collection has well over 1000 messages from people around the country, plus a whole collection in Quebecois French.



There’s something about the voice of a stranger on a phone line who has voluntarily left a message under the cover of dark anonymously, Oades says. What happens on The Nightline stays on The Nightline, she says – that’s part of its magic. Editor's pick Arts Saint. Martyr. Heroine. Next year the story of Joan of Arc will be told anew “I’ve been amazed by how open and authentic people are when they’re anonymous and it’s late at night. It’s a very open-hearted, intimate experience to receive these messages” There does seem to be a unifying quality to many of the visitors at that time, Oades says. “I think it’s also because all the noise has gone, and the only person left is you. It’s that they’re soul-searching about their own life.” The knowledge that you’re going to be listened to is important, she says, as is not being interrupted. That said, there is a real diversity to the calls. Some people become regulars, some even call every night.



One of Oades’ favourites is a garbage-truck driver from Warrnambool, who loves driving the streets at night, listening to Bruce Springsteen. “When he empties the garbage bins, he aims to put them back exactly how they were when he picked them up. So that when the people wake up in the morning, they’ll think, did those garbage men come? “Everything you hear in the work was genuinely left by a stranger in the night,” Oades says. “Nothing is made up.” The Nightline is at Malthouse Theatre from August 13 to 29. The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Babies are welcome at this Olivia Dean concert … as long as they have their own ticket
World.content:
BusinessConsumer affairsMotherhood Opinion Babies are welcome at this Olivia Dean concert … as long as they have their own ticket Bethany Williams Freelance writer August 11, 2026 — 7:30pm

August 11, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Olivia Dean’s music will always feel like summer to me. I first heard her voice in December 2022, at a dinner party in Manly. My friend had bought Dean’s debut album Messy on record as a gift for his girlfriend. As he pulled it from the magenta sleeve, Olivia’s signature gold tooth flashed at me from the middle of her perfectly blurry portrait. My friend grinned at me as he positioned the record and lowered the needle. “Trust me, you’re gonna love this.” For the Olivia Dean concert, Bethany Williams’ baby needs his own ticket. Jamie Brown Fast-forward nearly four years and Olivia Dean’s music has been embedded into my day-to-day and big life moments. A live band covered Dive while those same friends who introduced me to her music signed their marriage certificate. She has soundtracked road trips, housewarmings and dance parties in the living room with my toddler. And last September, as I shakily picked up a pregnancy test with a very faint but unmistakable second line, her collaboration with Sam Fender, Rein Me In, was filling our kitchen and spilling out onto the balcony. Forever when I hear that song the feeling will come back to me: the seasons changing, the weather warming, and finding out I was going to have another baby. The same week I discovered I was pregnant, tickets for Olivia Dean’s Sydney arena tour went on sale. My two sisters and I spent the morning on FaceTime, all of us waiting in the online queue, desperate not to miss out. We were delighted to secure three tickets, and the year-long countdown began. Now here we are, two months out. That positive pregnancy test has turned into a beautiful, chunky three-month-old baby with the best smile and the sweetest temperament. Having moved from inner-city Sydney to the Central Coast, I knew attending the concert would require some logistical planning. Afterpay Arena (formerly Qudos Bank Arena) has some understandably strict bag policies, so I sent an email explaining that I would have a young baby with me, and wanted to check that a pram and a nappy bag would be allowed through by security.



The response was prompt and positive. A pram would be allowed in but would need to be left in the cloakroom. No drama. A small bag with nappies and wipes would be permitted, as long as it wasn’t a backpack. Very considerate. But the clincher was in the very first line of the reply: “Thank you for your enquiry. For the Olivia Dean event, all patrons must hold a valid ticket for entry, regardless of age.” Bethany Williams and her baby son. I read it several times to be sure, and there was no mistaking what they were saying. Babies are welcome but they need their own ticket. I hadn’t even thought to ask if my baby would be allowed in. Because, well, he’s a baby. He’ll be less than five months old on the day of the concert. Our tickets are seated and he’ll be strapped to my body the whole time. Because he can’t sit. Because he’s a baby. Now, I should note that if leaving him at home with my husband was an option, I would happily take it. How anyone chooses to feed their baby is completely personal, and breastfeeding is all that is working for us at the moment. To separate my infant from my body would be to deprive him of sustenance for the seven-ish hours it will take me to get to, attend, and get home from the concert. I quite like my baby, so I won’t be doing that.



The only other option currently available to me is to miss out on one of my favourite artist’s concerts, which I have been looking forward to for more than a year, because I didn’t purchase a ticket for my unborn child when they went on sale. I can’t quite work out how to make sense of this. I know we are living in a time of bottles and daycare and nannies, and I think all of those things are wonderful and have their place. But on the flip side, a mother should still be allowed to choose to have her baby close, no matter the context, particularly if that baby is breastfed. In November 2025, Olivia Dean famously pressured Ticketmaster into issuing partial refunds to fans who bought inflated resale tickets, and forced future resale tickets to be capped at the original price. I can’t help wondering what she might have to say about a stadium demanding a seated ticket for a baby. I’m acutely aware of how our culture isolates mothers by being utterly intolerant to the inconveniences caused by children and babies in public spaces. I could write a whole other piece about that. But this is a far less complicated, borderline laughable conversation. My five-month-old baby, who will be strapped to my body, is absolutely allowed into the Afterpay Arena for Olivia Dean’s stadium tour as his first concert. He’s even allowed a pram and a nappy bag in the cloak room. He just needs to make sure to buy his own ticket first.



Bethany Williams is a writer who lives on the NSW Central Coast. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Trump’s vaccine order adds more fuel to the anti-vaccine fire
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's White House Trump’s vaccine order adds more fuel to the anti-vaccine fire Apoorva Mandavilli , Dani Blum and Maggie Astor August 11, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order calling for scaling back the number of vaccinations American children receive. At an Oval Office event announcing the order, Trump suggested falsely that vaccines were linked to autism and that the combined measles, mumps and rubella shot could be lethal, among other claims. The executive order by Donald Trump, pictured with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr, may not have any legal power, but it normalises misinformation about vaccines. AP While it is not clear yet whether the order has any legal power, experts are warning the statements from Trump, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr and others at the event could sow further doubt and confusion about the safety of immunisations. Here is what the evidence shows on some of those claims.



Combined measles, mumps and rubella shot is safe and convenient Trump has directed health officials to split the measles, mumps and rubella vaccines, which are currently given as a combined product, into three separate shots. “Together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal,” he said. Related Article Measles outbreak Revealed: Why measles is circulating undetected in Sydney There is no evidence that the combination MMR shot is dangerous, and many decades of evidence for its overall safety. It is associated with a small risk of seizures if a child develops a fever, but that type of seizure — which can occur after any high fever — does not cause long-term harm, according to the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. Individual vaccinations for the three diseases are available in some countries, but would need to be tested in the United States before they could be administered. Requiring parents to take their children in for multiple visits may deter some from getting the required shots.



Splitting the MMR vaccine serves “no medical purpose and would force parents to make multiple appointments, needlessly take time off work and make childcare arrangements”, said Dr Richard Besser, a former acting director of the CDC. Aluminum is safe and beneficial in vaccines Related Article Vaccination Florida to eliminate all childhood vaccine mandates, calling it ‘slavery’ The executive order calls for alternatives to the small amounts of aluminum used in some vaccines, which Kennedy has persistently claimed are unsafe. But aluminum salts, which have been used for nearly 100 years in vaccines to induce a stronger immune response, have been thoroughly studied for safety and efficacy. Clinical trials conducted over many decades support the use of aluminum. One study published in 2022 suggested a possible association with asthma, but it was small, and the study’s methodology meant it couldn’t show cause and effect. A second study, in Denmark, did not find a link with asthma or any of dozens of other disorders.



A narrower schedule could cause serious harm Trump maintained that “nothing bad can happen from what we’re doing”. But many diseases have been kept at bay in the US by high vaccination rates. A study published in 2024 by the CDC found that for children born from 1994 to 2023, routine vaccinations “prevented approximately 508 million cases of illness, 32 million hospitalisations and 1,129,000 deaths.” As vaccination rates decline, some of these diseases are coming back, most obviously measles: less than two-thirds of the way through 2026, there have been more measles cases than in any other year since the disease was declared eliminated in the US in 2000. Lower vaccination rates in the US have allowed a number of diseases to make a comeback. Bloomberg The executive order lists vaccines that it says should be recommended only for high-risk children. On that list are vaccines that protect against several diseases that can be fatal for anyone, including hepatitis A, hepatitis B and meningococcal disease.



The number and volume of childhood shots are not cause for concern Trump emphasised the volume of shots given to children, at various points calling it “the size of a bottle of soda,” “gallons” and “vats of vaccine”. Spacing out shots would “let time elapse between visits, so the body can handle this massive amount of fluid being pumped in”, he said. It is unclear what Trump is referring to. Most shots contain between 0.25 and 0.5 millilitres of fluid, roughly one-twentieth to one-tenth of a teaspoon. He and Kennedy said American children get 72 shots. In fact, even including vaccines that are recommended and not required, such as a yearly flu shot, children would receive about 35 shots by the age of five. The idea that today’s vaccines are overtaxing children’s immune systems is fundamentally flawed, experts have said. Vaccines today are cleaner and more efficient, and they contain far fewer stimulants to the immune system – by orders of magnitude – than they did decades ago.



Vaccines have been well studied on their own and in combination White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. AP Stephen Miller, a top aide to Trump who appeared at the event, said about the childhood vaccine schedule: “Nobody has studied it. Nobody’s looked at it. Nobody’s thought about it.” But for decades, a panel of advisers to the CDC typically spent months or even years reviewing data on new shots before issuing recommendations on which should be given and when. A federal court in March prevented that committee from meeting, saying the handpicked advisers Kennedy appointed to replace committee members he had fired were not qualified to make vaccine recommendations.



All vaccines must meet strict requirements for safety before approval. Even after their approval, federal officials monitor reports of side effects in multiple systems that analyse medical records and reports from patients and doctors. The shots in the schedule have all been closely studied, said Dr Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics. “The timing of them and the grouping of them has also been very well studied,” he said. Studies have shown no link to autism Trump and Kennedy suggested the cumulative impact of childhood vaccinations was driving rising rates of autism. While diagnoses have increased over the past several decades, scientists think a confluence of factors may be behind this trend.



Related Article Autism Trump blamed autism on this pain pill. Now, the gold-standard evidence is in Those could include people having children later in life, which is associated with a higher risk of autism, as well as more awareness about the condition and a broadening of the diagnostic category to include milder cases. But dozens of studies have not found a link between vaccines and autism. Autism experts believe multiple factors, including genetics and possibly environmental influences, play a role in causing autism. Kennedy has pledged to investigate the “root causes” of autism. Still, federal scientists have not released any new conclusions about what causes the condition. This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

World.title: ‘Lost a mill, but gained a Millie’: Elliott sees lighter side of Dogs’ exit
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘Lost a mill, but gained a Millie’: Elliott sees lighter side of Dogs’ exit Christian Nicolussi August 11, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Adam Elliott’s astonishing return from injury for the Rabbitohs will continue on Friday when he tries to end the NRL finals’ hopes of the club that cut him loose during the COVID pandemic. Elliott parted ways with Canterbury at the end of 2021 after a well-documented incident in a Gold Coast restaurant with Millie Boyle, the NRLW star who would later become his wife. Adam Elliott and wife Millie Elliott. NRL The forward still had two years to run on his deal worth $1m. “I lost a ‘mill’, but gained a ‘Millie’,” a smiling Elliott said at South Sydney training on Tuesday.



“There’s no animosity towards the Dogs at all. But I do think about it sometimes. My journey has been my journey. “There are things I would have liked to have done differently, but I’m here now, standing on my two feet, and I couldn’t be happier with my life, my wife and my family.” The fact Elliott is standing at all is remarkable considering he suffered a sickening ankle injury in round 12, and was told he would not return until October, when his one-year deal with the Bunnies was due to expire. The 31-year-old’s left ankle ballooned and was black and blue as a result of a ruptured deltoid and avulsion fracture of his tibia. Dr David Carmody and Souths’ Dr Andrew McDonald told Elliott his season was over.



But Elliott had missed the second half of last season with a biceps injury, and refused to accept he was facing another lengthy stint out of the game. Adam Elliott is looking to finish the year strong with Souths after overcoming a serious ankle injury. NRL He spent countless hours in a hyperbaric chamber, embraced red light therapy, and overhauled his diet, including eliminating fatty food and seed oils. “I was meant to be in a boot for four weeks, and basically learning how to walk again – but I was out there running on the field after three weeks,” Elliott said. “I went against a lot of the advice at the start, and butted heads with people who only had my best interests at heart. I understood it and appreciated that. But I needed to take a risk to get back and play.



“It didn’t feel too bad when I was running, and a couple of weeks after that I was back running in boots out on the field. “[Coach] Wayne [Bennett] kept laughing at me because I kept telling him, ‘I’ll be back soon’. “I had a job to do. This is my 12th year in the NRL. I didn’t want to let anyone down. I suffered a biceps injury last year, two weeks after my father passed away. It was a tough time. I didn’t want footy taken away from me again, and I couldn’t let it be the case here. “If you’re passionate about something and believe in it enough, and believe in yourself, you can make it happen.”



Bennett has seen some remarkable comebacks during his coaching career, including Souths’ skipper Cameron Murray’s push to return from an achilles injury to make a final-round cameo last year, and was amazed by the work Elliott had put in to defy the odds. “They told me he wouldn’t play again this year, but he got out there and did things nobody thought he could do – it’s been quite remarkable,” Bennett said. “He wanted to play football again and not let his teammates down.” The Elliotts last year welcomed daughter Gigi. Millie said: “He was told he’d be out for the season, to not get his hopes up because it was such a significant injury, but he didn’t want to accept that, and he never had it in his mind he was not coming back. He’s lucky to have me, but I’m so lucky to have him.” Elliott will start in the back row on Friday night, directly opposite Jacob Preston, who was not at Belmore before Elliott exited. Campbell Graham returns from a calf injury on the right wing. Victory will all but seal a finals’ berth for the Bunnies, and leave the Dogs four points adrift of the top eight.

World.title: Two new cities join the race to host the 2028 NRL grand final
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Two new cities join the race to host the 2028 NRL grand final Adrian Proszenko August 11, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Melbourne and Auckland are the latest cities to express an interest in hosting the 2028 grand final, sparking the biggest bidding war ever for the game’s showpiece event. The 2028 decider is up for grabs at a time when a scheduling clash with Pope Leo XIV’s Sydney visit may prompt a change of date or venue. NSW Premier Chris Minns has indicated he wants the match to remain in Sydney, but will face stiff opposition from rival Australian states. Five cities are in the mix to host the 2028 NRL grand final: Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane, Perth and Auckland. Matt Willis Melbourne is the latest to publicly state its intentions, joining Sydney, Perth and Brisbane in jockeying for the hosting rights. There is also the prospect of the match going offshore for the first time after New Zealand expressed an interest in pinching the game. It raises the possibility of the fixture leaving the harbour city for just the second time after the COVID-19 pandemic restrictions resulted in it being shifted to Brisbane’s Suncorp Stadium in 2021.



Melbourne set the record for the biggest State of Origin attendance when 91,671 fans packed the Melbourne Cricket Ground for the second game of this year’s series. “When the world’s biggest sporting events look for a home – they choose Melbourne,” said Victorian Minister for Major Events Anthony Carbines. The view inside the MCG during Origin II this year. Getty “That’s because everyone knows that Melbourne is the events capital of Australia – not Sydney or Brisbane. “We’ll continue conversations about a wide range of events that pump millions into our economy and create more jobs.”



New Zealand will host its first State of Origin match next year at Auckland’s Eden Park, and the city is hopeful that could be a springboard to hosting the grand final the following year. “It would be fantastic if the NRL grand final was in Auckland in 2028 and we are all looking forward to next year’s State of Origin game at Eden Park, which is sure to be a huge success,” said Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown. “The Warriors’ continued success has generated enormous excitement, and Auckland’s appetite for rugby league right now is insatiable.” Rugby league is booming in New Zealand, courtesy of the remarkable rise of the Warriors. Coach Andrew Webster’s side has emerged as a genuine contender after upsetting premiership favourites Penrith on the weekend. The NRL is likely to introduce a 20th team into the competition in 2029, with a New Zealand-based team the most likely option.



Related Article Exclusive

NRL 2026 The premier, the Pope and the boss: NRL grand final up for grabs “Auckland has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to deliver world-class events, supported by outstanding venues, a new city rail link, and a fan base that embraces major sporting occasions,” said Annie Dundas from Tātaki Auckland Unlimited, the events arm of Auckland Council. “While the NRL’s plans for future grand finals are ultimately a matter for the NRL, Auckland would naturally be very interested in exploring opportunities that align with our strategy of attracting major events that deliver economic, tourism and community benefits for the region. “For now, our focus is on working with our partners to make State of Origin 2027 a memorable event for fans, teams and visitors from Australia.” Queensland Premier David Crisafulli on Monday stated Suncorp Stadium’s case for hosting the decider, saying: “It would make complete sense for the NRL to choose Queensland and we will continue to put that case forward.”



The grand final bidding war kicked off in earnest when WA Premier Roger Cook revealed to this masthead that his state would “bid hard” for the rights. Sources not authorised to speak publicly due to commercial sensitivities said the Western Australian government was prepared to pay $20 million to host the grand final, which is almost twice as much as that offered by NSW. Australian Rugby League chairman Peter V’landys said on the weekend he felt a sense of loyalty to the Minns government, “but as a business, we have to look at every option.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.
